THE MARRIAGE. Blest be they who, hand in hand, Joined in wedlock's holy band, Enter now another sphere, One in which they each may cheer, Soothe, and sway a loving heart, Sure of love till death them part. Sweetly glide their years, and may Each return of bridal day Indicate, beyond a doubt, Perfect love will fear cast out ; Ever free from carking cares, Health, Peace, Competence, be theirs.' EDWARD N. Minas.

SONNET. I hold that day apart from all my days. A wan disastrous light was on the sea, And o'er the moors the rain crawled drearily. We heard no plover pipe about the place. Or shift his lonely tune a little space Across the drenched hollows, where the bee All Spring and Summer through went questing free To drop and feed upon the gorse-gold's blaze. Only the rain-drip in the birch, the sigh Of the sere heather-bells that lingered yet, The arrowy swirl where tarn-born torrents met And tossed and whitened with a windy cry ; But it was then you called me "friend,' and high Above all days and years that day is set. •rv". Varittio. When a pretty Irish girl is stolen away, they suspect Some boycotter. A medical writer says children need more wraps than adults. They generally get more. A fool in high station is like a man in a balloon. Every- body appears little to him, and he appears little to every- body. " Mr. A. is one of those people who rob Peter to pay Paul." said Mr. B. " Hardly, hardly," responded Mr. C. "Oar friend A. doesn't do that exactly. He always stops after roboing Peter." Conversation on a see.side hotel veranda between a young ran and an elderly guest :—Yoang man: "I must have arn yen s enewhere, sir ?" Elderly guest: "Very likely I am a pawnbroker." The only form of oath among the Shoshone Indians 14 The earth hears me, the sun hears me—shall I lie?" "And then," says a Western paper, "the big chief does lie with double-barrelled mendacity." Mn. Mixer hoe discovered the respective natures of a distinction and a difference. She says that "a little differ- ence" frequently makes many enemies, while " a little distinction" attracts hoses of friends to the one on whom it if, conferred. A conceited young fellow, calling ripen an old lady friend previous to his departure for China, was taken somewhat by surprise when the good-natured old lady advised him to be careful of himself in the "flowery kingdom," as she under- stool the Chinese feasted on puppies. A Celorado paper tells of a flock of sheep the black wool Of which was turned white in a single night by terror. Next we shall hear from Nevada of a man whose homespun coet grew white between days on account of the fright of the sheep from which the wool for the coat was clipped. %,-A.LXINO PECULIARITIES.— —Walking appears simple en e:eb, and yet, somehow, not one person in a hundred seems able to perform it with ease—indeed, it would not be difficult in a single morning's stroll to find materials enough to construct a volume on the subject of "How motto walk." Till 6 person ambles, that one strides like a camel; a third, whose form is nearly spherical, cannot, perhaps, do other than roll; a fourth patters along upon his toes; a fifth de- termined to avoid so absurd a mode of progression, minkeeps his toes well up and his heels well down, as if deecetling a Steep hill—in fact, nearly every person we meet either creeps, or hobbles, or slides, or trots, or limps, or jumps, or resorts to one form or another of what a pulpit orator once, Inn fine leue,t of eloquence, termed "peripatetic artifices." , Grace ought to be as natural to man as to other living crea- tures, and yet he is assuredly the most awkward animal in creation. A HAND TO HAND COMBAT IN THE WEST Bow.—A bitter personal quarrel had existed for some years between miss Johnstone of Westerhall and Hugh (from his balk generally known as Braid Hugh) Somerville of the Writes, and they had often fought with their swords, and parted on eeu d terms. Somerville, in the year 1596, chancing to be in Edinburgh on private business, was one day loitering aboat the head of the Bow, when, by chance, Westerhall was seee ascending the steep and winding street, and at that neweent some officious person said, "There is Braid Hugh Swnerville of the Writes." Westerhall, conceiving that his enemy was lingering there either in defiance or to await him drew his sword, and crying, "Turn, villain!" gave Somer- ville a gash behind the head, the most severe wound he had ever inflicted, and which, according to the" Memoirs of the So mervilles," was "much regrated. ettirwards by. himself." s Writes, streaming with hlood, instantly drew his word, and ere Westerhall could repeat the stroke, put him sharoly on his defence, and being the taller and stronger man of the two, toeether with the advantage given by the slope, he pressed him sorely. Keeping on the defensive, Westerhall gave way step by step, seeking to gain the advantage of the aecent and thee supply the defect of his stature, which Writes perceiving, be bore in close upon him hand to hand. Thue they continued in close and mortal combat for about a quar- ter of an hour, "clearing the causeway," so that none conid venture near them or leave the shop doors; neither dared any man attempt to part them, for every thrust and stroke of their swords threatened all who came near. Westerhall eventually was driven down fi elating every inch of the way to the foot of the Bow, and having on—for riding, probably —a pair of long black boots drawn close up, was becoming quite weary, and stepping within a shop door, stood there on his de!.-nce; and then the last stroke given by Hugh Somerville nearly broke his good sword, as it struck the iStrme lintel of the door, where the mark remained for years after. "The tonne being by this tvme all in an uproar," they were separated by a party of halberdiers, and conveyed to their lodgings. Their wounds were slight, save that whieh Writes had just received on his head, from which several pieces of bone came away. After he was cared, and after the death of Hugh Lord Somerville, Privy Councillor to James VI. (an event which occurred in 1597), these combat- ants were reconciled, and their feud committed to oblivion. —" Cassell's Old and New Edinburgh." AN Anainaer Fanren.—ln an article in the Gentleman's Magazine there is a story of an unsuccessful fox in the fable' Of "The Fax and the Crow," which sounds familiar enough to English ears, but has no point of resemblance to the tale in which the fox is acted with that strange yearning after a piece of cheese. In the Arabic story, the tables are turned upon this fox, who certainly deserved some punishment for his behaviour to his children. Every time he had a child, Bays the Arabic fabulist, he ate him, waiting, howevee, with judicious self-control, till he was full-grown. At the top of the mountain, at the foot of which this fox dwelt, a crow had built her nest. With this crow the fox determined to estehlish a fraternity, on the grounds of their neighbour- hood and their common profession of Islam. The crow, an experienced bird, objected that this brotherhood would pro- bably be rather of the tongue .than of the heart—such a brotherhood, in fact, as was between the eater and the eaten. The fox, however, professed to allay these scruples by the tale of" The Mouse and the Flea." A mouse had established herself in the house of a rich merchant. One night a flea arrived at this merchant's couch, and, being athirst, drank his blood. The merchant sat up alarmed, and, making a loud outcry, summoned his servants and his neighbours. Thereupon they hastened to him, and, tucking up their sleeves, commenced to search for the ilea, who turned and fled, till she came to the mouse's habitation. The mono', on being supplicated to accord the fugitive a refuge, ex- perienced in her tarn some little anxiety as to her own saf sty ; but, eventually, being quieted by the solemn asser- tion of the flee that no harm should happen to her, granted the asylum prayed for. She, however, advised the flea to be abstemious in the matter of the merchant's blood, and quoted some elegant verses to the effect that there is great advantage in seclusion and content with the gifts of Provi• dence, even though those gifts be no more than a morel of bread and a draught of water, a tattered coat and some Coarse salt. The flea then passed the day with the mouse, and the night with the merchant, taking of him only just enough to sustain life. At last the merchant brought one day a quantity of deenars, w';ich, before sleeping, he hid under his pillow. The mouse waxed r&ghtily anxious to possess this wealth, and aeeed the flea to assist her with some device. " How can I be of any service," answered the flea, " who am not able of my own strength to remove a single deenar ?" However, slis made off at once to the merchant and gay him a fearful bite, such as she had never before given him. The merchant turned on his side, and the flea gave him another bite, worse than the first. Upon this the merchant, on. the peevish pin, left his bed, and went to sleep on the stone bench outside his house. Then the mouse, in extreme delight, fell to removing his deenars. "And such reward As this," concluded the fox, " may be thine for thy good action to me, 0 acute, intelligent, and discriminating crow !" The crow's parsnip's, however, were not to be buttered by any faalt words, and he replied to the fox with, another fable of the sparrow, in which he intimated thee the old fox was measuring himself with one too strong for him. This rami- fying, by the way, of one fable into severel others, is of a piece with all the tales in the "Arabian Nights," and in- bd ee 71, c'ew,iintht te6 originalve rfr'arapeowloogrku , quoting Here i eascuhp thepooi f his own sentiments. The sparrow, flying by chance over a While sheep-cote, stops to consider it. eagle carries off a young lamb. The hsplearrow' doing a ns iom, aatelda large the force of example, lights on the back of a fat ram and endeavours to emulate the ea,,Yle. His feet become entangled in the wool, and so far he is from executing his design,that he cannot escape from the shepherd, who ties a string to his foot and presents him to his children for a plaything, tell- erg them, when they ask, "What thing is this ?" "This is he who measured himself with one too strong for him." " Such may be your case, 0 fox I" concludes the crow, Hand good day to you." BUILDING SOCIETIES. —A return just issued shows that in Eagland and Wales there are 394 old building societies in existence, and 873 societies which have been formed since 1874, making a total of 1,267. The membership of 1,015 of these societies amounts to 372,035, giving an average of 367. The receipts during the last financial year of 1,115 societies amount to £18,694,555. The liabilities of 1,111 societies amount to £21,813,095 to the holders of shares, and £14,079,762 to depositors and other creditors. The balance of unappropriated profit in 903 societies is stated at £1,104,735. There is a balance deficit ifn the case of 167 societies amounting to £47,209. The assets amount to £36,950,383. Al' JETRUT OF DEAN STANLEY.—AS one looks back on him, the "study of imagination" gets thronged with pic- tures, that pass gently before "the eye and prospects of the soul," recalling that slender figure, "that good grey head," that beautital counteibance, amidst the old familiar scenes that shall know him no more for ever ;—in the pulpit of the choir, or at the,reading-desk in the nave, as in the summer twilight he pronounced, in his tone of trembling earnestness, his benediction of that "peace of God which passeth all understanding"; among the chapels and the monuments, the tiny centre of a listening ring of visitors—often of work- ing men—to whom he is imparting the lore of the mighty Abbey; in the Deanery, in quiet talk in his study, or in rich and versatile colloquy at his table, in those bright days when the gracious presence, that he was so proud of, shed its charm on all; at St. Andrew's, in the oil library, on the everung of his installation, searching out each of the stud- ents for a word of talk, and at last resting by the table, in the centre of the room, and saying, with an air of satisfac- tion and relief, "Now, I think I have spoken to every one"; —all now but a vision and a memory. He was one of the few rum whose transparent moral goodness, purity, simpli- city, united to intellectual strength, seemed to others to be a guarantee of the reality of that better world of serener air, in whose high regions the pure forms dwell, "above the smoke and stir of this dim spot which men call Earth."— R. H. Story, D.D., in Good Words. 'LIE POPULATION OF THE GLOBE.—According to MM. Behm and Wagner's Berakerung der Erde, Europe has now a population of 315,929,000 inhabitants •, Asia, 834,707,000; Africa, 205,679,000; America, 95,405,000; Australia and Polynesia, 431,000; the Polar regions, 82,000; giving a total of 1,455,923,000, being an increase of 16,778,000, according to the latest known censuses. At the end of 1877 Germany had a population of 43,943,000, Aus- tria and Hungary (1879) of 38,000,000, France (1876) of 36,900,000, Turkey in Europe of 8,860,000, Russia of 87,900,000. In Asia, China possesses 434,900,000 inhabi- tants, Hongkong 130,144, Japan 34,300,000, according to the census of 1878. The British possessions in India number 240,200,000 people (an estimate made before the census of this year), the French possessions 280,000, Cochin China 1,600,000, the East Indian islands 34,800,000, the Wands of the South Sea 878,000. The area of Africa is estimated at 29,383,000 square kilometres divided el, I ol- lows : —Forests and cultivated land, 6,300,000; savannahs, 6,235,000; steppes, 4,200,000; deserts, 10,600,000. The inhabitants of British North America number 3,800,000, of the United States 50,000,000, of Mexico 9,485,000, and of Brazil 11,100,000. The Polar regions extend round the Arctic Circle with an area of 3,859,000 square kilometres, and the Antarctic regions about 600,000. The population of the former is small, with the exception of Iceland, which has 72,000, and Greenland 10,000. ,

A conference an the subject of land reform in Scotland will be held at Aberdeen on the 6th of October. A whole row of gild-fashioned houses was destroyed by fire on Tuesday in the village of Carisbrooke, Isle of White. As the result of the revision of the borough voters' lists at Sheffield, the Liberals claim a net gain of 426, whilst the Conservatives claim a net gaictof 237. An accident has occurred to a ballast train on a dew line I of railway in lowa now in course of construction. Three of the workmen were killed and thirty injured. After the marriage of Mr. Howard. and Lady Emily Eary, some thieves succeeded in carrying off from the house of Lady Charleville the whole of the bride's diamonds. 1 Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., the Earl of Roseberry, and Sir F. Herschell will take part in the opening of the New- castle-on-Tyne Junior Liberal Club, towards the end of October. 1 Manchester figures in the unenviable position of being at the head of the mortality returns for the great towns last week, with a death-rate of 25 per 1,000 per annum, Bradford being the lowest with a rate of 15. Liverpool was not far below Maachester, the rate being 23 per 1,000. At Sheffield on Sunday a runaway horse dashed into a crowd drawn together by a " service ' given by the "Salva- tion Army." Many persons were knocked down and trampled upon, and nine, mostly children, were seriously hurt. John Mills, miner, was charged before the Barnsley magis- trates, on Tuesday, with assaulting Hannah Eccles by throwing a quantity of vitriol and powdered glass into her eyes, seriously injuring he'r. Miles and Eccles had kept company for some time, but the latter had since married another man, Mills was committed for trial. The magistrates at OxfsSid on Tuesday had before them applications for the renewal of the licenses of the pub- licaes scheduled at the recent Commission. The Mayor announced that six of the applications would be granted, and the other six were refused. Notice of appeal was given. SUICIDE OF A JEALOUS Loven.—On Tuesday, at Long- ton, vi Minn Wootton, a young man, committed suicide by hinging himself to a wall outside his own house'. A policeman, who cut the body down, discovered a letter, in which deceased declared his lovei for a girl named Alice Berksand, showing jealously to have been the cause of the rash act. Sir Stafford Vorthcote. in a letter to the secretary of the Oldham Conservative Working Men's League, denies the accuracy of the report that at Sheffield he expressed ap- proval of the Irish Land Act as it now stands. He states that Cie bill, though containing some good and some very bad provisioits, is founded on a wrong principle. He has no confidence in it, though, as the bill is now law, it should have a fair trial. Two conflicting decisions as to the operation of the Welsh Sunday Closing Act were given on Tuesday. At the Hawarden petty sessions several publicans were •fined for Sunday trading, the magistrates bolding that the operation of theact Was immediate. At Swansea, where the stipen- diary magistrate had consulted the Home Secretary on the 'subject, it was held that the act does not come into opera- tion until next year. ' A shocking affair happened on Tuesday at Gloasop, re- sulting in three deaths. Mrs. Downing, wife of a respect- able workman, took two of her children—an infant son and a little girl aged three years—from the house, and soon afterwards the dead bodies of all three were found in a mill lodge cloee to the town. Since the birth of her infant the unfortunate woman had betrayed symptoms of mental aber- ration, and her rem:nal to a lunatic asylum was in contem- plation by her friends; but, unfortunately, they had not ca•ried out their intentions. A Wnr.sw VICAR IN s WESLEYAN PULPIT.—On Sunday evening, the vicar of Penstrowed, near Newtown, Mont- gorne-yshire, was walking in the neighbourhood of a Wesle •an chapel in his parish, and the preacher of the evening not having been punctual, the officers of the chapel invited the vicar to take his place in the pelpit. The vicar acceded to the request, and preached a sermon which highly pleased the congregation. He expressed great regret that there should be so wide a breach between Churchmen end Nonconformists as regards their religious worship, and, our correspondent has been informed, expressed his willingness to occupy the Wesleyan pulpit on future occasions. The circumstances have given rise to a good deal of gossip in the county. Bank notes of the value of £9OO have strangely dis- appeared during their transmission through the post from Inverness to Balmacarra, in the west of Ross-shire. It ap- pears that on Wednesday last a letter, addressed to the agent of the Commercial Bank at Balmacarra, containing £9OO in - Commercial Bank notes, was put into the post office by the agentof the Commercial Bank of Scotland at Inverness. One of the first things which arrests the attention of any one who studies the Land Question is the great monopoly which practically exists. Years ago this fact had frequently been referred to by such statesmen as Mr. John Stuart Mill, Mr. John Bright, and others, but byatheir po- litical opponents and those connected with what is known as "the Landed Interest" (i.e., those who receive the rents, not those who have to get their living on the land either as farmers or labourers), their statements as to the comparatively limited number of landowners were treated as exaggerations. Finally, however, the Earl of Derby broached the subject in the House of Lords, and the result was the preparation by Government officials of a return, arranged in counties, of the landowners of the United Kingdom, the acreage of their estates, and the estimated rental. The metropolis was, how- ever, not included, although its rental is estimated at equal to one-fourth of the rental of the rest of the United King- dom, outside the metropolitan area. In other respects also the Blue Book is very misleading, as, for instance, if a man owned two estates in different counties he was put down as two landowners. In this way the Duke of Buccleuch is put down as 14 landowners because he owns property in 14 dif- ferent counties. Eminent men have, however, gone tare. fully through this important Government return, and, by infinite labour' have extracted and compiled the pith of the information. Mr. Arthur Arnold, M.P., tells us that accord- ing to this "New Doomsday Book" 525 persons own one- fifth of the United Kingdom. The House of Lords owns over 15 millions of acres, with an estimated rental of over £12,000,000, and this does not include estates of peeresses, or the forest lands and woods (except salable underwood s) nor all the estates held by trustees, while it is known that the estimated rental is too low by at least one-fourth. Neither does this Blue Book include the vast extent of com- mon and waste land, the bulk of which is claimed by these great lords, nor is any land included which is not rated for the relief of the poor; in fact, Mr. Arnold asserts that the property of the nobility amounts to nearly one-fourth of the extent and to one-eighth of the estimated rental of the United Kingdom. So much for the House of Lords. But there are great landowners outside that House amongst our country gentry, and those who have carefully studied the figures of this complicated "New Doomsday Book" have no hesitation in saying that four-fifths of Great Britain and Ireland are in the hands of somewhere about 7,000 persons. According to Mr. Brodrick :—ln the county of Lancaster 10 Peers own 135,222 acres; 36 great landowners (i.e., Com- moners owning at least 3,000 acres, if the rental reaches £3,000 per annum) own 218,570 acres; 79 squires (i.e., owners of estates between 1,000 and 3,000 acres) own 134,300 acres; 257 greater yeomen (i.e., owners of estates of between 300 and 1,000 acres) own 128,500 acres; 692 lesser yeomen (i.e., owners of estates of between 100 and 300 acres) own 117,640 acres; 10,845 " small proprietors" (i.e., owners of over one acre and less than 100 acres) own 168,100 acres; 76,177 cottagers (that is, owners of under one acre) own 14,811 acres; 639 public bodies own 30,221 acres ; and there are in this populous county 64,305 acres lying waste, including places like Chatmoss, making a total of 88,735 owners and 1,011,769 acres. The question naturally arises how is it that this enormous extent of land has accumulated in the hands of such a com- paratively small number of landlords. How did they get the land in t first instance? Some of our great landed families possess estates which have come down intact from Norman times when the country was parcelled out among the Conqueror's followers. Other families have almost in each generation married the heiresses and "broad acres" of other old families. Some like the "Russells" or Dukes of Bedford shared largely in the spoils and "fat-...ands" of the Burnish Church in the reign of Henry VIII., while not a few of the founders of our modern nobility have invested the enormous fortunes made by trade, in estates, to give them power and qualify themselves for the Peerage. But how have these big estates been kept together? The explana- tion is simple. Since the introduction of the Feudal System into this country by the Normans, the landlords have al- ways been the governing body. We have already seen how entirely the House of Lords is a house of landlords, while to-day in our so-called "Radical" House of Commons there are 173 landowners with nearly two millions of acres, and an estimated rent roll of £1,732,560. There are also 160 members of the House of Commons connected with the Peerage either by birth or marriage, or are Irish Peers themselves. 'rhe Land Laws from time immemorial have been made by land!ord s, who, to use a homely expression, have always taken care "to have the blanket-on their side of the bed," or as a recent writer has well said—" Our Land Laws as a matter of history were made by the aristocracy, and interpreted by the lawyers for the aggrandisement mainly of the aristocracy, and not for the preservation of the people." This was natural, and we may say necessary, for it is one of the most trite maxims of political science that any class of persons entrusted for long periods of time with unlimited and irresponsible power are sure to abuse it. Hence the gradual diminution of small proprietors, the absolute un-existence in Great Britain of one of the best classes in all communities—the peasant pro- prietors—and the maintenance of laws of heritable succes- sion and certain forms of heritable conveyance, which prac- tically tend to lock up the land in the hands of a few, and to remove it in a great measure out of the vital circulation of the community, and thus we are found at the present ' moment standing pretty nearly in the same position that Rome stood in when Pliny wrote the famous sentence: " Latif undia perdidere Italian' Our big estates have ruined Italy.'" The two great means by which these big estates are kept together when change of circumstances, or poverty, or mis- fortune, or bad management, or immorality would otherwise bring them ioto the markzt are "Primogeniture" and " En- tail." Primogeniture as a law only applies to landed pro- perty where the owner dies intestate or without a will. En- tail by settlement or will is Primogeniture as a custom, and will be dealt with in a subsequent article. Primogeniture, or the right which belongs to the eldest [Child, particularly to the eldest son, had its origin long long I ago, when the circumstances of the country, and of society, I were altogether different from what they are to day, and may be said to be now entirely obsolete and out of date. Although there is some little doubt as to whether it was in- troduced by William the Conqueror as part of his Feudal system, it has certainly been in operation in this country for more than six centuries, and gradually replaced (except In Kent) the old Saxon law of Gavelkind, by which a free- holder had a full right to alienate his land by sale or gift, and to dispose of it by will, hi default of which it was equally divided amongst his children. According ,to the great Adam Smith in his "Wealth of Nations," the original lacquisition by a few individuals of uncultivated lands, tthough a great might have been but a transitory evil. They might soon have been divided again, and broken into small parcels either by succession or alienation. The law of Primogeniture hindered them from being divided by suc- cession, the introduction of Entails prevented their being broken into °small parcels by alienation. When land, like movables, is considered as a means only of subsistence and enjoyment, the natural law of succession divides it like them among all the children of the family, all of whose sub- sistence and enjoyment may be supposed equally dear to the father. This natural law of succession accordingly took I place among the Romans, who made no more distinction be- tween elder and younger, between male and female, in the 1 inheritance of land than we do in tho distribution of movables. But when land was considered as a means not I of subsistence merely, but of power and protection, it was thought better that it should descend undivided to one. In those disorderly times every great landlord was a sort of Petty prince. His tenants were his subjects. He was their judge, and in some respects their legislator in peace, and their leader in war. He made war according to his own dis- cretion, frequently against his neighbours and sometimes against his Sovereign. The security of a landed estate, therefore, the protection which Its owner could afford to those who dwelt on it, depended, upon his greatness. To divide it was to ruin it, and to expose every part of it to be oppressed and swallowed up by the incursions of its neigh- bours. The Law of Primogeniture therefore came to take place not immediately, indeed, but in process of time, in the succession of landed estates, for the same reason that it has generally taken place in that of monarchies, though not always at their first institution. That the power and con- sequently the security of the monarchy may not be weakened by division, it must descend entire to one of the children. To which of them so important a preference shall be given must be determined by some general rule, founded not upon the doubtful distinctions of personal merit, but upon some plain and evident difference which can admit of no dispute. Among the children of the same family there could be no indisputable difference, but that of sex and that of age. The male sex is universally preferred to the female, and when all other things are equal, the older every- where takes precedence of the younger. Hence the origin of Primogeniture and of what is called lineal succession. "Laws freguently continue in force long after the circum- stances which first gave occasion to them, and which could alone render them reasonable are no more." In the present state of Europe the proprietor of a single acre of land is as perfectly secure of his possession as the proprietor of 100,000. "The right of Primogeniture, however, still con- tinues lobe respected, and, as of all institutions.it is the attest to support the pride of family distinctions, it is till likely to endure for many centuries. In every other respect nothing can be more contrary to the real interest of a nume- rous family than a right which in order to enrich one beg- gars all the rest of the children." The signs of the times to•day are rather different from what they were when Adam Smith wrote his book 100 years ago, and the continued existence of the law of Primogeniture is simply dependent on the question as to how BOOD public attention is thoroughly directed to it. For a matter of fact legal definition of Primogeniture we will now take Williams, who, in his "Real and Personal Property," says, " Privaogeniture, or the right of the eldest was among the males to inherit, was a matter of far greater con- sequence in ancient times, before alienation by will per- mitted , than it is at present. Its feudal orig.n is undis- puted, but in this country it appears to have taken deeper root than elsewhere, for a total exclusion of the younger sons appears to be peculiar to Engl,;nd ; in other countries some portion of the inheritance, or some charge upon it is in many cases at least secured by law to the younger sons." In another place Williams says, Primogeniture as a cus- tom has been the subject of much remark. Where family though property large iw n h the descends e honours or family estates are to be preserve&some such device under passage ' intestacies,‘ Tthheou appears necessary. In the 2nd vol. of the same work ap- pearesndts to he following aggregate, is generally small in individual rases. When the wishes of all cannot be consulted, that which would have been the wish of the generality of intestates ought

apparently to form the foundation of the rule. From a consideration of these circumstances the reader may per- haps be induced to think that if, in case of intestacy, the rules for the devolution of real and personal estate were identical, and with some slight variations, similar to those which now exist as to personalty, the law on this subject would de rendered both more simple and more just." So much for the great conveyancing authority who after naively admitting that its chief use is to preserve family honours, or family estates, and thereby serve family pride, pleads that though the real property of intestates is large in the aggregate, it is small in each case, but that perhaps it would be as well if in those cases it were treated like the same value in money woald be, i.e., divided amongst the next of kin fairly. Exactly, that is just what is required, regardless of the family honours" or "family estates." If there was only one case in Great Britain where primogeni- ture operated as it does now in the event of intestacies it would be none the less a wrong to those who suffered by it, and ought to be prohibited by law. The great objection to the Law of Primogeniture in the case of intestacies is its gross injustice. Scores of cases Might be quoted where great hardship has been incurred in consequence of its operation. Although the writer has per- sonally known several such, it will be sufficient to illustrate the matter by quoting one which is given in a recent work by Mr. Arthur Arnold, M.P. A tradesman who saved money had made a will in his wife's favour. Whilst he was in good health, they agreed together that his savings should be invested in a farm. He accordingly attended a sale by auction, bid, became the purchaser, and paid the deposit re- quired by the auctioneer. He died before the purchase was completed. His widow, the sole executrix of his will, to whom he intended to leave all the savings of their joint. . thrift and industry, was of course compelled to complete the , purchase. Upon that being accomplished, the entire pro- , perty was claimed, and was obtained, by a nephew, in ac- cordance with the law which in England governs the in- . heritance of land. The widow was left destitute, and ulti- : lately became chargeable to the parish for poor-law relief. , It has, been truly said that "The Law of Primogeniture never works but to work an injustice." And yet, although a series of attempts have been made by various members of Parliament during the last 40 or 50 years to assimilate the devolution of real estate to personal property on intestacy, and thus to abolish the "law" as dis- tinct from the "custom," it is still on the Statute-book, and we, in enlightened and civilised England, are a long way behind our own Colonies, and the great American Republic, in still retaining this antiquated piece of feudalism. In 1836, and again in 1837, Mr. Ewan moved for leave to in- troduce a bill with this object, whereby nndevised realty would have vested, like personalty, in the executor or ad- ministrator, but was defeated on both occasions. The struggle was renewed again and again by Mr. Locke King from 1850 to 1869, in which year he actually obtained a ma- jority in favour of a bill providing that where any person beneficially entitled to any real estate shall die without a will that estate shall pass to his executor or adminis- trator, and shall be either divided or sold exactly as f it were personalty for the benefit of creditors and the next of kin. A " Real Estate Succession Bill "

of the same general character was announced in the speech from the Throne and introduced by the Govern- ment in the session of 1870, but was not pressed beyond the first stage, and the promise given to re-introduce it was not redeemed. Another bill introduced by Mr. Locke King and Mr. Hinde Palmer in the session of 1873 embraced within its definition of real estate every kind of property which is not personal estate. This bill never even came on for discussion. The " Real Estate Intestacy Bill" intro- duced by Mr. T. B. Potter in 1876 and rejected on the lsecond reading by 210 to 175, was based on the original bill of Mr. Locke King. The Law of Primogeniture in the United Kingdom therefore still remains such that in case of the death of a landowner without leaving a will, the whole of his land goes to his eldest son, without the slightest legal claim of the widow (unless she happens to be entitled to dower) or the other children to a single penny, even should that land constitute the whole property of the deceased. Were such a principle applied to personal property such as furniture, money, &a., it would lead, as Mr. John Bright has said, "to immediate confusion, and, by destroying the whole social system, to a perfect anarchy of property. Why, then, should that course be followed with regard to land ?" When the voters of our large towns will cease to return members identified with that party who wish to keep things as they are, and the farmers have learned that to vote for "the Squires" is the best method of stopping all reforms, however necessary and beneficial, we shall be much nearer the abolition of the present Law of Primogeniture.

Spring cleaning has no terrors for the watchmaker. At the theatre one evening, behind the scenes, Suet 9b. served a performer put something under his cloak, and asked him what he had got there. "Oh, only my dagger," answered the player. Suet, however, drew out a small bottle, and having ascertained that it contained his favourite bever- age, drank the contents, and returned him the bottle with these words—" There's the sheath."

St. Thomas Aquinas being in a closet with Innocent IV. when an officer brought in a large sum of money, produced by the sale of absolutions and indulgences, "You see, young man," said the Pope, "the age of the Church is past in which she said Silver and gold I have none.'" "True, Holy Father," replied Aquinas, "but the age is also past when she could say to a paralytic, Rise up and walk.'" NOBLE Dos.—The very land of dogs, and the land wherein the dog receives most genuine honour, and himself rises to his noblest development of character, is unques- tionably England. It is to be deplored that the greatest English poet never drew the character of a noble dog, and condescended to degrade his pen by the miserable caricature of Launce's cur • bat since Shakspeare's days our poets have done what in. them lay to make up for the omission. Cow- per, Walter Scott, Burns, Byron,Tennyson, the two Brown- ing% and Matthew Arnold, have all been eminent dog. lovers, and have written tender things of dogs, living and dead. English history is full of records of dogs—noble dogs of Charles I. and Kenelm Digby ; pitifully faithful dogs, like the little creature which accompanied Mary Queen of Scots to the scaffold, and laid itself down between the severed head and beautiful neck; silky spoiled favourites, like the spaniels of Charles. 11., and Diamond, the dog of Sir Isaac Newton, which gave the great philosopher a year's extra trouble by destroying his papers.

_ BULLS OF ALL NATIONS.—It was a Scotch woman who said that the butcher of her town only killed half a beast at a time. It was a Dutchman who said that a pig had no marks on his ears except a short tail. It was a British magistrate who, being told by a vagabond that he was not married, responded, That is a good thing for your wife." It was an English reporter who stated at a meeting of the Ethnological Society that there were "casts of the skull of an individual at different periods of adult life, to show the changes produced in ten years," though Dean Swift cer- tainly mentions two skulls preserved in Ireland—one of a person when he was a boy, and the other of the same per- son when he grew to be a man. It was a Portuguese mayor who enumerated among the marks by which the body of a drowned man might be identified when found—" a marked impediment of speech." It was a Frenchman who, con- tentedly laying his head upon a large stone jar for a pillow, replied to one who inquired if it was not rather hard, "Not at all, for I have staffed it with hay." It was an American lecturer who solemnly said one evening, "Parents, you may have children, or, if not, your daughters may have." It was a German orator who, warming with his subject, ex- claimed," There is no man, woman, or child in the house, who has arrived at the age of fifty years, but what has felt the truth thundering through their minds for centuries." It was an English lawyer who drew up an indictment in which the prisoner at the bar was charged with killing a man with a certain wooden instrument called an iron pestle. It was Peter Harrison, a commentator on the Pentateuch, who, in explaining the table of stone on which Moses wrote the Commandments suggested that they were probably made of a peculiar kind of wood. GREENWICH TIME.—It will be obvious that a sun-dial made for London would be useless for either Paris or Edin- burgh. The altitude of the Polar star varies with the lati- tude, and hence is greater at Edinburgh and less at Paris than at London; and as the style must always point to the Pole star, the angle it makes with the dial plate must vary with the latitude. Again, a little consideration will show that before clocks and watches came into use there would be no such thing as Greenwich time. At the present day, no matter in what part of the British Islands we may happen to be we regulate our watches by Greenwich time, which can always be ascertained at the nearest railway-station. But when dials had to be depended upon, different towns would have different time. London time would differ from that of Bristol, Glasgow from Edinburgh. It has been al- ready stated that a place fifteen degrees to the east or west of Greenwich has noon an hour earlier or later, as the case may be; and if fifteen degrees make an hour's difference, one degree will make a difference of four minutes. Thus, it is noon at Greenwich eight minutes before noon at Liver- pool, and five-and-twenty minutes before it is noon at Dub- lin. Of course people might agree then, as now, to accept Greenwich time as the standard; but then where would have been the use of their sundials? Probably a uniform standard of time was not so necessary two or three cen- turies ago as it is now, with onr railways and telegraphs and all the complex life of modern civilisation. A survival of the old custom of each town having its own local time still exists at Ipswich, where the town clock indicates local time, and is therefore always about four minutes before Greenwich time.—Science for All.

THE LATE PRESIDENT GARFIELD.
TRH PUATERAL.

The remains of the late President Garfield were on Friday, after a special serve, relneved from Washington to Cleve- land, and there Werra on Monday. The manifestations of public sympathy in this country arising out of the death of the President have assumed a widespread form. On Sunday reference to the sad event was made in most of the pulpits of the land, and on Monday signs of moarning—in tolling bells and partially closed shops—were pretty general in most of the large towns.
THE REMOVAL CV THE REMAINS TO CLEVELAND.-PREPARA- TORT SERVICE AT WASHINGTON.

-- • -- --- Mrs. Garfield and her family took a last view of General Garfield's remains on Friday afternoon, staying about 30 minutes. Everyone else retired while they communed with the dead alone. The Society of the Army of Cumberland, who had been guarding the caskel, then re-entered the Rotunda, and the funeral ceremonies commenced. Mrs. Garfield and family were not present. Every available seat was speedily occupied, and when President Arthur entered the entire assemblage rose to honour him. After they had resumed their seats. the Rev. Frederick Power began the services by giving out the hymn, "Asleep in Jesus, which was impressively sung, the sound reverating through the dome far above. The Rev. Dr. Rankin, of the Congrega- tional Church, ascended the platform at the head of the catafalque, and read appropriate selections from Scripture. The Rev. Isaac Errett prayed. Dr. Power then pronounced the eulogy upon the illustrious dead,the service closing with prayer by Ike Rev. J. G. Butler. The funeral ceremonies ended about four. When the casket was removed to the hearse, which was in waiting to receive it at the eastern portico of the Capitol, the spectators moved out of the Ro- tunda, Many, taking places in the procession. A few moments afterwards the procession started, a military escort preceding the hearse, which was followed by a long line of carriages two abreast. The hearse having halted, the casket was taken to the train inside. The distinguished occupants of the carriages then alighted. Vast crowds lined the entire route, men reverently uncovering their heads as the hearse passed. With as little delay as possible the train started, moving slowly out of the station at 5-21. A second train, containing members of Congress, followed eight minutes later. The bells were tolled in every town through which the funeral train passed, the people standing with uncovered heads at all the stations to get a glimpse of the casket, whereon rested the Queen's wreath. The railway track at York was strewn with flowers throughout the town, while, for eight miles through Pittsburg and Allegheny, flowers had been strewn at intervals on the track. The floral offer- ings on the half-mile of the park were especially handsome, extensive flower beds having been Asstily arranged on the green sward alongside the railway. At one town hundreds of people were kneeling, and every house was draped with mourning white. At Sellersville the coal miners came out of the pits with lighted lamps on their hats, standing in a Iline by the roadside. The train arrived at Cleveland at 1-30 on Saturday afternoon, the second train arriving at 1-50. Countless multitudes were atanding with uncovered heads as it entered the suburbs. The Caninet alighted at the station. all uncovering while Mrs. Gartield, leaning on her eon's arm I and escorted by Secretary Blaine, went to her carriage. Twelve artillery sergeants then took the casket on their 1 shoulders, carrying it to the hearse. The Commit- tee of the Society of the Army of Cumberland, with General Sherman and Sheridan and Admiral Porter, followe' the coffin to the heard. Four negroes were at the horses. heads, and moved the hearse out into tha•kinclid Avenue The same men performed a like office at the same place for President Lincoln 16 years ago. The occupants of the fune- ral train then entered the carriages which were waiting, and the procession moved at about two o'clock through the densely crowded avenue, a vanguard of police preceding it. Colonel Wilson led the way. He was followed iv a band ; then came a troop of cavalry; then the carriages with Governor Foster and the Committee of arrangements; then came the Columbia Coramandery of Knights Templar at Washington, of which General Garfield was a member. The hearse then appeared, flanked by the artillery sergeants and followed by a drum corps and the Cleveland Commandery of Knights Templar. The most conspicuous feature of the procession then followed, being the surviving veterans of General Garfield's old regiment—the 42nd Ohio—less than 100 in number, bearing its tattered and Worn battle flag. A double column of carriages, containing the Cabinet. the Guard of Henour, and members ef Congress, concluded the procession. It moved slowly along Euclid Avenue through an indescribable scene. The magnificent avenue was draped in mourning throughout, with General Garfield's portrait on almost every house front. The street was crowded with silent and mourning people. No sound was heard but dirges and the tolling of the bells. The procession turned into Erie-street, then through Same-. Templarh e an n carrying incri inclined it' a nor-street, to Public-square. Over one hour was occupied in march. When the hearse stopped the sergeants took betweethent c ih e lines onf e the There he te Knightsth the casket was deposited, with the Queen's wreath reeling on the head of the coffin, and palm branchesat the foot. The catafalque rested upon a platform aft high, approached by uense canopy r inclined walks. An imt ose above it. On either side of the catafalque were banks of elaborate floral designs sent by Cincinnati there was also a profusion of flowers is exquisite designs.l Such an imposing floral array had rarely been seen in this country. The catafalque was fairly smothered in floral gifts, above which rested the black coffin', with the Queen's wreath surrounding it. The work of decoration of the cata- falque and pavilion was not completed until late on Satur- day night. General Garfield's portrait was placed stove the coffin, it being decided that the remain, should not be ex- posed to view. The entire square was illuminated by electric lights. The coffin, with its surmounting wreath, was plainly seen from the surrounding streets. Beneath General Gar- field's portrait on a scroll was the inscription : Vie's race well run; Life's work well done; Life's crown well won; Now comes.rest.

Throughout Sunday the populace, in solemn procession, marched through the pavilion, viewing the casket, with its floral decorations. The Queen's wreath was a prominent object of attraction, many remarking," God bless her." There were remarkablie manifestations of mourning along the route. In the larger cities ,thousands gathered silently on the arrival of the train, the stations were draped with black, bells being tolled, and salutes fired. All through the country the spectate. s assembled on the sides of the railway with uncovered heads, some even kneeling. The line in some places was strewn with flowers. SnoCEING ACCIDENT ON TILE ROAD TO CLEVELAND. The newspaper reporters left Washington for Cleveland on Friday night, in a special train, by the Baltimore and Olio Railway. Early on Saturday morning, when 35 miles west of Pittshurg and while crossing a trestle bridge, the train ran into a handesr carrying nine railway labourers. One jumped from the bridge into the creek, 0 feet below, escaping with several broken bones; one was unhurt, while the other seven were killed. They disobeyed orders by goinz on the bridge before the train. The survivorssaid they knew this, but took their chances.

div.head: 'VIEWING THE COFFIN.
div.p: 'VIEWING THE COFFIN.

CLEvntssia, Monday.—The forest city—for so Cleveland is called from the wealth of foliage that surrounds it—is a city of sorrow, whose broad streets and grand avenues of spreading elms are to-day draped in the blackest mourning 1 weeds. The arrangements for the late President's funeral I attracted to the town on Sunday visitors by every train, all eager to make their pilgrimage to the grave in Lake View Cemetery. How they found accommodation and lodgment is a mystery. All through the Sunday evening and all through the night people passed in an unbroken stream of four abreast past a catafalque. During the day and night nearly two hundred thousand mourners must have walked past the bier between the grim files of soldiers who guarded the way. Rain fell in theafternoon, but that made no difference to the crowd. That did not break up or even perceptibly diminish the great, long lines of mourners, extending half a mile on either side of the entrance to the f ur.eral pavilion, patiently waiting for their turn to view the coffin. The most remarkable fact in connection with Sunday's pro- ceedings was the number of little children who appeared on the scene. They were deeply affected, and the spectacle was one that can never fade from their memories. Their parents had taken advantage of the occasion to impress upon thorn a due sense of the value of those honest, old- fashioned virtues which had found so much vigorous expression in the daily life of the late President. The little ones were awestruck, and in some cases seemed rather fright€4o. Yet it is a characteristic illustration of the domesticity which is a feature in the American character, s round the coffin was cleared by the soldiers, that even the children 0 the Republic were on Monday made to share in a great demonstration of national feeling. A large Pace and in a temporary way fenced off. For nearly half a mile on either side, east and west, lines of troops kept the passage open. Between these the crowd filed in the most perfect order day and stream, and when it grew dark the scene was illuminated by night, four abreast in one long unbroken electric lamps. But two persons each second passed the bier, so that the enormous number of pilgrims may be easily estimated. Scarcely a sound was heard save the tread of the crowd and the low moaning of the wind through the trees. div.p: TIM EXAMINER, SATURDAY. OCTOBER 1, 1881.

rounded the house where he stopped, and waited long and patiently merely on the offtchance of catching a glimpse of his bright, handsome face and erect, martial manner. The great funeral procession was marshalled in nine divi- sions, the first six divisions comprising contingents of militia and soldiery sent by the various states, including the State Governors, members of various orders, friendly societies, students* societies and clubs, veterans who fought in the civil war, representatives of Roman Catholic, Irish, and various other societies, organised bodies of citizens, municipal deputations, dm, dec. The seventh division con- sisted of the Funeral Escort proper, and at its head marched the Washington Marine Band. It included a bodypf Cleve- land Horse, the funeral car, and a fine detachment pt Federal Artillerymen. This division also included the pall- bearers, which were Professor Wm. J. Streaton, the Hon. B. Lockwood, I. H. Rhodes, H. C. White, Hon. R. P. Ramsey, Hon. J. W. Tyler, Edwin Cowles, D. P. Ellis, Hon. Be C. Parsons, Selah Chambsrlain, William Robinson, and Cap- tain C. E. Henry. They were chosen not on account of their professional and social position, but sitnply because they were Mr. Crarfield's intimate personal friends. They were distinguished from the restsof the procession by their white silk badges. The platform of the funeral car was sup- ported on heavy wheels. Its measurement was eighty feet by sixteen. From its edge to within one inch of the ground there floated heavy black drapery, bordered with a silver fringe. Heavy fads of white silk, caught up on black silk cords, also ornamented the rest of the body of the car. Two terrace steps led up to the pall. Between these steps rows of immortelles ran around the whole car. At each corner of the platform stood flags draped in black. The erased canopy was supported by three columns on each side, all covered with black broadcloth. Garlands of immortelles were coiled round these columns, the capitals of which were Egyptian in design. Immediately above the columns there , ran a projecting cornice studded with black and white rosettes.. From the subjacent frieze hung rich festoons of heavy silver 'fringe. On the four corners above the canopy black ostrich plumes waved in the breeze. The dome of the canopy extended six feet above tPe cornice, and was covered with black cloth surmounted by immortelles. On the cor- nera of the dome beautiful black plumes also waved. The whole structure was crowned by a great funeral urn wreathed with immortelles. In the ceiling of the canopy alternate folds of black cloth, white silk, and bright red trappings were hung. The casket on the dais containing the body was covered with black broadcloth, bordered along its upper edge with immortelles. The car was drawn by twelve black horses, four abreast, which were led by six negro grooms. The horses were caparisoned with heavy black. cloth covers bored with silver fringe, and bearing on their heals white-tipped plumes. To clear the way for this car branches of the trees lining the stately Euclid Avenue had to be lopped off. The Eight Division consisted of car- riages in which were seated the Guard of Honour, consisting of Generals W. T. Sherman, P. H. Sheridan, W. S. Hancock, and R. C. Drum, Admiral C. S. Porter, .Paymaster Looker, Surgeon-General P. S. Wares, Commodore Earl English, the ex-Presidents of the United States, the members of the Cabinet and Diplomatic Corps, the Judges of the Supreme Court of the United States, the Senators, the Governors of States and their staffs. There were also in this Division Members of Congress, the Society of the Army of Cumber- land, Mayors of large cities, and distinguished guests in; vited by the Secretary of State. To the Ninth Division, consisting of the Ohio National Guard, was as- signed the duty of keeping the line of march. It fell ' into the procession, and brought up the rear when the Eighth Division had passed. Minute guns were fired during the march. Upon arriving at the cemetery the mighty column halted, and, opening 'its ranks, faced in- wards, and reverently saluted the remains of 0,0 dead After the funeral service was over it counter-marel.ed, and was diamissed upon its ieturn to the Monumental Park. Dr. J. P. Robinson presided over the funeral services in the forenoon in the Mohumental Park. They consisted simply of singing by the Vocal Society, reading passages from the Scriptures by Bishop Bedell, the offering up of prayer. another service of song by the Vocal Society, an address by the Rev. Isaac Erritt, the reading of a hymn by Rev. Jabez Hall, more singing, and finally the solemn benediction, pro- nounced by Rev. C. S. Pomeroy. At the grave, Chaplain H. Jones, of the 42nd Ohio Regiment, officiated. He offered up ft brief but earnest prayer that struck a responsive chord in the hearts of every one in the mighty multitude of mourners gathered together in the cemetery. After that there was some singing of sacred music by • the Gellman Singing Sozieties, and the Benediction was pronounced by President Hinsdate, of Ithaca College. Nothing could ex- ceed the simplicity of these proceedings, and yet their effect was solemn—we might say awe-striking. The vast crowd of mourners, with uncovered heads and grief stricken counten- ances, was electric with suppressed feeling. At the supreme moment when the body of the illustrious dead was 'com- mitted to the earth, one almost feared that this emotion would find expression in some loud and piercing cry of pain. But even then the countless company of mourners stood, to. all outward appearance, calm and self-restrained, sorrowing but silent. Mr. Garfield's wife and mother and children at- tended the funeral ceremonies at the Pavilion. They drove to the grave behind the funeral car. They will go to Mentor immediately. The estimates of the numbers present run to two hundred and fifty thousand, who must have all wit- nessed the procession, which was little less than two hours in passing a given point. It marched in open order at the rate of two miles an hour. Many in the procession were totally exhausted by the heat and fatigue. Refreshments were freely dispensed to all. Water was supplied from every fir_ plug on the route, and so the day's discomforts were partially lessened. The coffin has been deposited in the re- ceiving vault, and will remain there until a built-in grave can be prepared. Over this will soon Hack noble monument. Services in honour of the deceased Fresident were held throughout the Union, and business was suspended. THE FINAL INTERMENT. The Standard's correspondent at New York says :—The body of the late President is, properly speaking, not 'buried yet. It is laid in the vault, the entrance to which is loaded with decorations, but this vault is not, in its present con- dition, the last resting-place of the coffin. The grave to which it is ultimately to be consigned is specially built for its reception, but the massive masonry is not yet finished. The final interment will be a matter of family arrangement. Mrs. Garfield's wish is that it shall be strictly private. In the circumstances It is certain that no one will intrude upon the sorrow of those nearest and dearest to the late President when they perform the last offices to the dead. The coffin is now strongly and strictly guarded. A detachment of the 'Ohio National Guards are told off for this sacred duty. It is feared that the corpse might be stolen and subsequently held to ransom by scoundrels, as was done in the case of the late Mr. Stewart. There was an attempted robbery of Mr. Lincoln's tomb planned five years ago. The authorities are thus forewarned, and they .will take care to prevent the pos- sibility of such an outrage being perpetrated by baying the coffin deeply imbedded in iron and cement. Mrs. Garfield and her aged mother-in-law are nervously anxious about this. The body will be it is said, subjected to some further process of embalming, to remove some of the discolouration of the features and to restore the face to something ap- , proaching its appearance during life. It is doubtful if this statement is more than an idle rumour. The proposal to subject the late President's face to public gaze again is strongly deprecated. When Mrs. Garfield covered it with her own hands in the Capitol it was understood that she wished no human eye to look upon her husband's face after hers. The general feeling is that her wishes in this respect should be considered sacred. It is highly Improbable, there- fore, that the coffin will ever again be opened.

pointment, as he miL:ht have to wait some time before it was intimated to hies officially. The President kept Guiteau's letter, which was afterwards shown to some of his friends as a sample of the man's presumption. Guiteau had for some time been paying his addresses to the daughter of a wealthy American citizen, but to no purpose. Presumably he was under the impression that a good position was all that he required in order to win the young lady's consent. As soon as he thought be had secured his appointment as Minister to this country he renewed his attentions, dwelling 'upon the advantages attached to the post which he supposed was about to be offered to him, and pressing for a favourable re- sponse to his suit. At last he became so importunate that the young lady's friends communicated with the police, and Guiteaa was made to understand that he must give up his indiscreet proceedings at once.

which we would think of no more; and as we stand round the open grave to-morrow sympathizing to the full with those that weep—all sympathizing, from our gracious sovereign lady to the humblest true heart amongst us—let us pray that in that grave may all past discords be buried, and that henceforward our rivalry may be one of brotherly love and Christian zeal."

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY DEMONSTRA.- SION..
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY DEMONSTRA.- SION..

A Standard New York telegram, dated Tuesday, says No one here seems to know how long the period of mourn- ing ought to be extended. This may lead to very awkward consequences. Last night a theatre opened its doors, the justification being that the funeral servicbs were over, and that therefore it was not indecorous to proceed with the per- formances. The result was that, in an incredibly short time, a furious mob assembled in front of the building and threatened to burn it to the ground. It was with the utmost difficulty that their indignation was assuaged, and that the police persuaded them to disperse.
ENGLAND TO AMERICA. ' (Front Punch.) JAMES ABRAIVI GARFIELD.

Born, November 19, 1831. Died, President of the United • States, September 19, 1881. Silence were best, if hand in hand, Like friends, sea-sundered peoples met; But words must wing from land to land The utterance of the heart's regret, Though harsh on ears that sorrow thralls E'en sympathy's low accent falls. Salt leagues that part us check no whit, What knows not bounds of time or space, The homestead feeling that must knit World-scattered kin in speech and race. None like ourselves may well bemoan Columbia's sorrow; 'Lis our own. • A sorrow of the nobler sort. Which love and pride make pure and fair; A grief that is not misery's spot, A pain that bows not to despair; Beginning riot in courtly woe, • To end in pageantry and show. The great Republic's foremost son Struck foully, fails; but they who mourn Brave life cut short, good work half done, Yet trust that from beyond death's bourne That blameless memory's gifts may be Peace, concord, civic purity. Scarce known of us till struck for death, He stirred us by his valiant fight With mortal pain. With bated breath We waited tidings morn and night. The hope that's nursed by strong desire, 'Though shaken often, will not tire. And now our sables type, in truth, A more than ceremonial pain. We send—court, cottage, age, and youth— From open hearts across the main Our sympathy—it never swerved— To wife he loved, to land he served I •

THE ASSASSIN GUITEAO. Telegrams from Washington state that the grand jciry, 011 meet on October 3, and will first take up the cases of the occupants of the gaol who are unable to obtain bail. This is Guiteau's position. Evidence will be heard first, then the indictment, will be brought, and then the pass will come into court. Guiteau has no counsel yet. If be has none when he comes to the Court, counsel will be assigned, and then an adjournment will have to take place to enable the counsel to prepare the case. It is not likely that the trial will take place before November. According to a telegram, from Vienna to the Daily Telegraph, Guiteau solicited the post ?f United States Minister to the Austrian capital. He unagined that it was to be given him, and accordingly ap- plied to General Garfield for private notification of his ap.

div.head: ST. HELENS SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.
div.p: ST. HELENS SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES.

On Friday night a free public meeting was held in the Town Hall, St. Helens, to witness the distribution of prizes and certificates to the successful candidates connected with the Science and Art Classes during the past session. The hall was well filled with an appreciative audience, and upon a screen at the entrance end specimens of drawing and sketching were placed, representing the work of about 40 student:, being the pupils of Mr. Abbott. The specimens, which were greatly admired, had been sent by the pupils to London for examination. On the platform were His Wor- ship the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alderman Johnson, Revs. R. J. Ward, T. Wilshaw, Canon Carr, A. A. Nunn, W. C. Tayler, J. Brown, W. Flaherty, Drs. McNicol and Twyford, Messrs. W. W. Pilkington, R. G. Brook, W. H. Foster, J. Burchall, T. Brewis, J. C. Gamble, Wm. Gamble, A. Sinclair, C. Culshaw. Amongst those in the body of the hall were Messrs. T. Cook. H. L. Riley, J. C. Bishop, and Dr. Jameson. The MAYOR said that as this was his first appearance in public since the lamentable death of President Garfield, he thought it WAS their duty to express their sympathy with Mrs. Garfield in her misfortune. Everyone present would. agree with him in expressing a vote of condolence with Mrs. Garfield in this great trial. He was quite sure they only expressed the feelings of the whole of England in doing so. (Applause.) His duty that evening was a very pleasant one, and that was to announce to them the presence of a distinguished visitor who had come there to distribute the prizes to the successful students on that occasion. He was glad to meet with so many of the relatives of the pupils, and he hoped that meeting would act as a stimulus to them in the future. He was also glad to state that the amount sutscribed had been greater than in any other year. That at all events was a very favourable aspect. It was also satisfact,ry to know that after providing for the local prizes there was something to carry forward to next year. To have an annual meeting like that he thought would be desirable, and he thought they would all agree with him. He did not think they could have any gentleman more eminently qualified for the purpose of addressing them at their annual meeting than their distinguished visitor, Sir James Picton, who had rendered immense and valuable services to the city of Liverpool. (Applause.) Mr. CULSHAW read the committee's report for the years 1879-80 and 1880-81, as follows :—ln presenting their report for the last two years, the committee have to congratulate the subscribers on the improved prospect there is at the present time, of the committee's work progressing satisfac- torily. Last year there was no public prize distribution; but the local prizes were distributed privately. To cover the cost of these a small number of subscriptions was col- lected, no appeal being made to the general body of sub- scribers. The committee have to thank the subscribers for their liberal response to.such an appeal just made. Owing to this, the committee are able to announce definitely the prizes they are prepared to offer for the ensuing session. A new feature will be introduced into the prize list: a silver medal will be gtven to the candidate who obtains the most and highest passes. The following prizes will be given to candidates who pass the Science and Art Department's ex- aminations, and are most attentive and painstaking in their Preparation studies :—ln any subject in which ten or more candidates pass, three prizes will be given, of the value respectively of 155., 10s., and 7s. od. Where less than ten, but five or more pass, two such prizes will be given. And where fewer than five pass, one prize. Both medal and prizes can only be taken by candidates who attend the classes regularly; and in making the awards, passes will not be counted which are a repetition of similar passes obtained by the same candidates previously. The following is the list of prizes: CLASSES HELD AT COWLEY SCHOOL.—Teacher, Mr. Wardlow. Sound, Light, and Heat.—ltchard Croston, first-class certificate and Queen's prize; Herbert Bamford, first-class certificate and Queen's prize; Thomas John Roberta, first- class certificate and local prize; John Morton, first-class certificate and local prize ; William Charles Taylor, certi- ficate; Henry Dutton, certificate. Mathentatics.—George Watkinson, first•class certifiate and local prize; Arthur E. Houghton certificate. . CLASSES HELD AT S. THOMAS' SCHOOL.—Teacher, Mr. Abbott. Steam and the Steam Engine.—Noah J. Borrows, first- class certificate, Queen's prize, and local prize. Certifi- cates :—Charles Lewis, Frederick Blackburne, and Jno Traverse. Freehand Drawing.—Henry A. Sherlock, certificate and local prize ; Alexander Porter, certificate. Model Drawing.—James Porter, certificate. Perspective Drawlng.—William W. Gandy, first-class certificate, Queen's prize, and local prize; John Dean, certificate. Geometrical Drawing.— Certificates and local prizes : Ellen Forshaw and James Porter. Certificates :—Alfred M. Booth, Harry H. Gandy, Henry W. Roaghley, Henry A. Sherlock. Works of the Art Class sent to London for competition.— A third grade prize, Henry A. Sherlock, viz., a small set of photographs from Ralphael Cartoons, in portfolio. James Porter, Alexander Porter, and Joseph Smith are mentioned in the Government report as having sent up good sets of drawings.

div.head: ENGLISH SYMPATHY.
div.p: ENGLISH SYMPATHY.

Everywhere throughout the United Kingdom, on Mon- day, touching tokens of mourning were visible in connec- tion with President Garfield's funeral. Special religious services were held in Manchester Cathedral and numerous other places of worship. In the London City Temple a memorial service was held, Dr. Joseph Parker officiated, assisted by the Rev. Newman Hall, and others. There was a crowded congregation. The pulpit wa& deeply draped in black. Madame Antoinette Sterling sang, "Beyond the silent and the weeping," and the "Dead March " in "Saul" was played on the organ. Dr. Parker, in a funeral address, dwelt upon the high qualities of the late President, the heroism of Mrs. Garfield, and the sympathy which had been manifested by this country. At the conclusion of the address a message to be forwarded to Mrs. Garfield was agreed upon, assuring her of the deepest sympathy under a bereavenaent which was borne by the whole civilised world. In Manchester business was to a large extent suspended in the Exchange and the leading warehouses. In Liverpool the cotton market was closed. In London the day was largely observtd as an occasion of mourning. The window blinds of all the royal palaces were drawn, the Stock Exchange was closed at noon, and in all the leading thoroughfares signs of mourning were plentiful. It is pro- bably correct to say that there is not a town in the kingdom in which the day was not kept in a befitting manner.

DISTRICT PULPIT REFERENCES. On Sunday, fitting allusion was made to the late President Garfield, in the prayers and sermons at many of the places of worship in this distlict. ST. HELENS. Preaching at the Parish Church, on Sunday morning, the Rev. Canon Carr LLD., took w for his text the ted.3,— " Boast not thyself of to-morrow, for thou knowest not What a day may bring forth (Prov. xxvii, 1 v.") The preacher said he had been led to choose this text by the melancholy event which during the past week had plunged the whole 'civilised world into morning—the lamented death of the President of the United States. Tracing the career of the late President, the, younger portion of the congregation were especially directed to the fact that General Garfield com- menced tile in the very humblest way. As an 4istance of the extreme poverty of the Garfield family he mentioned that when the President was about four years of age his elder brother, who had commenced to earn wages, was en- abled to buy him a pair of shoes—a comfort which he had not hitherto enjoyed. Very early in life he exhibited a taste for learning, which was gradually acquired through many difficulties, and he became a self-educated man, which, after all (the rev. canon considered), was the best kind of education. From a learner lie became a teacher ; one a teacher he became a professor, and while a professor, he was proud to say, he also became a preacher of the Gospel. He was a God-fearing man--which indeed he had been all through his career—and just before his death lie is reported to have said to his successor, " Jam not afraid to die." The late President Garfield was an example worthy of imitation. Canon Carr then referred to the close relations of England with the United States, and expressed a hope that this event, melancholy though it was, would bind the nations more closely together, and that out of the evil good might arise..—The organist (Mr. W. B. Woodward) played the "Dead March " in " Saul" at the conclusion of the service. At the Congregational Chapel, Ormskirk-street, the Rev. Professor Scott, LL.D. of the Lancashire Independent Col- lege, specially prayed LL.D., the sister nation, that the bereaved fami:y might be upheld, that the contemplation under which the wicked deed was committed might be very far from realised, and that the bonds of unity between the British nation and America might be more firmly cemented to- gether.—At the close of the service the " Dead March " in " Saul " was played as a tribute to the late President's memory, the congregation remaining. INDEPENDENT METHODISTS AND THE LATE PRESIDENT. On Saturday afternoon a convention of ministers and representatives of the Free Gospel and Independent Churches was held at Zion Chapel, Liverpool. Mr. W. Oxley, of Manchester, president of the connexion. presided, and in his opening address alluded to the death of General Garfield, who he said was in connection with a church much like theirs, that recognised no paid agency except the support of evangelists. General Garfield was known in the church as Bro. Garfield to the end. Mr. Brimelow, of Bolton (con- nexional editor), then moved—" That this conference, com- posed of ministers and representatives of the United Free Gospel Churches, desires to express its profound sympathy with Mrs. Garfield and family in the loss she has sustained through the lamented death of her husband, and prays that God will strengthen and bless her in this dark hour of trial ; and also desires to tender their most sincere sympathy with the American people in this sad event."—Mr. W. Sanderson, of Liverpool, seconded the resolution, which was carried in silence, the conference standing.
