So in source of wealth to the community. That is briefly the our two nations. Differences our fathers had, which we history of the town down to a recent period. How it got the would readily forget; a misunderstanding we have had, name of St. Helens is a mystery. The present church is

dedicated to St. Mary. Whether there was a chapel called St. Helen is a question, because the town is called in some of the old documents St. Mary-in-Helen. However, be it So, it is a very respectable name, and very much to be revered; because I believe Helena was the mother cf Con- stantine, who founded the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem. So that you are of very respectable parentage. The present town of St. Helens, what shall I say abou that? If I were to say it is a handsome town, equal M Oxford or Edinburgh, YOU would think that I was poking fun at you. (A laugh.) I do not say so, because I do not thins it is. I can say, with ' all deference to Col. Gamble and those who are connected with the trade, that while it is not a superior town, it is in- dustrious, public-spirited, wealthy, and progressive. If you do not agree with that, then you are hard to please. It is a very enterprising place; and you have in St. Helens an excellent specimen of English life, self-dependent--self- assertive if you will—active, industrious, thrifty, thriving, and go-ahead. The evidences of that are pretty easily forth- coming in the increase of the population. I believe the population of St. Helens has doubled itself, during the last 14 years, and now amounts to about sixty thousand. I be- lieve, out of London, you are the largest community in the kingdom without parliamentary representation. (Cheers.) In this town of St. Helens, however smoky it may be, and however repulsive we may say it is in some respects, there is a large amount of philanthropy and enterprise, and of everything that tends to further your progress in life. The very existence of the institution, the anniversary of which we are celebrating to-day, is a witness of it. In regard to religion you have places of worship of every denomination that exist in the Christian Church, and not the least is that venerable body of Quakers, who have had a great deal to do in founding the prosperity of SCPtelens in times past. In regard to philanthropy you have institutions, hospitals pro- vided for the old infirm, the sick and destitute, and you have by no means been unmindful of education. One, Sarah Cowley, whose name ought to be honoured in this locality —(applanse)—many years ago left an estate, which is fruc- tifying and increasing in value each year. I was shown that magnificent building to-day, and I was not quite grati- fied to And that it is lying there like a ship ready to be launched, but wanting the funds to launch, it. When the Great Eastern was built they could not launch her, and they had to spend £70,000, in addition to the thousands ex- pended in its construction, to launch the ship. Here this magnificent school cannot be opened for the wait of a thousand pounds. Well now, really what ip £l,OOO. If ten gentlemen gave one hundred each, or one hundred gave ten pounds each, it would be done. You have only to publish it in the Market-place of St. Helens, and lots will be willing to subscribe the money at once. And this will be done; it is really a question of time, and with a long pull, a strong pull, and a pull altogether, you will open the doors with edit, and carry on an enterprise with every prospect of success. Let us see what the future of St. Helens may be and ought to be. You are entitled to parlia- mentary representation, and I have not the least doubt when the next arrangement of boroughs takes place you will get one member, and perhaps two. (Cheers). You are fairly entitled to it, and I have not the least doubt you will get it. Whether the member be Whig or Tory I care not, but God speed him, if he represents your interests, whether he be one or the other. That is one point in which I think you will be sure of progress in the future. With regard to the beautifying of the town—(hear, hear)—you have got some very nice buildings in the town, this one is a very handsome building, and this room appears to me—l don't know whether lam heard at, the other end of the room,—but it appears to me to be a good room to speak in and I trust it will be made use of in literature, art, and science. (Hear, hear.) I am told that you have no School' Board. " What " I said, "A large town like this without School Board?" "Ah " said my informant "the reason is, we do not want a School Board, because there is abundant provision without any School Board at all." I think there are verY few towns in the king- done of anything like this size, of which that can be said. (Applause). In Wavertree, we have 10,000 inhabitants, but we have ample accommodation without any School Board at all. You have got your science and art classes, and I have looked over the report given me with great pleasure, and you seem to embrace a vast variety of subjects, and if pro- secuted with energy and good-will cannot but be effective and powerful for the future. There is one science, that of chemistry, which seems especially to belong to you for there Is Be .reely an occupation carried on here but depends more or 1 .3 on chemistry, such, for instance, as smelting copper; the . inufacture of glass, and the making of alkali. All i the- 'hinge are connected with chemistry, which should I the. .re be thoroughly understood. I believe in your cut ilum this is fully provided for. Science has a great ' de,t_-- tore in store for us in the way of discovery; our , mtet-rjv over the powers of nature is yet comparatively in , .icy. There have been wonderful discoveries, but 1 there yet to be effected the utilisation of the black smoke i that ,w ascends into the air, and also the utilisation of i those npurities known as noxious vapours. I have no i doubt but that both of these will be found to be useful 1 articles turned to man's ure and enjoyment with the advan- tage of purifying the air we breathe, and.making our town salubrious and healthy. Ido not blame St. Helens for its clouds of smoke; it is natural to the town, and it enriches the community, and nobody has a right to complain. But the time will come when by the advance Of science we shall do all these things ander a pure atmosphere and serene sky. As to the question involved in the prizes given out, and the studies they represent. I have spoken of man's conquests over nature; but there are other conquests in which man has to take a part, and to carry out great designs, and that , Is the conquests over himself. Man does not live for him- self alone, nor by himself. We live as 1 said before, by our 'conquests over nature. 13ut then there is a mental world in which we are all partakers, where conquests may be obtained, where progress and influence may be procured, and where man will rise to a higher region of content, industry, and progress than anything which the physical world can afford. The physical sciences are merely the means to an end, and that end should be progress in moral and intellectual eminence. Without that all our progress in the arts and sciences will be utterly vain. Let us now say a word to the young friends to whom we have had the pleasure of giving , these prizes. (Cheers.) You have now tasted something of , the sweets of the reward for the diligence you have displayed in your studies, and I trust , what you have gained is merely the stepping stone to-the advances you will make in the future. There are two or three cases which have recently occurred particularly , interesting, to which one cannot help making allusion. We find in a free country likeoars men rising up from thelowest walks of life, and by activity, tact, aptitude, and diligence, making a place in the world, and doing credit to the country to which they belong. I will just call attention to two, and point a moral in a few words from them. The first f will take is Sir Josiah Mason', of Birmingham,—(applause)-- , an example of what energy, sagacity, and integrity will do. •Until 30 years of age everything he undertook always ' failed. But he married an admirable woman for his wife who comforted hint, cheered him on, and told him he must go to the front eventually if only he persevered. At one time they were reduced to such straits that they had not a meal to eat. The wife, who was a clever cook, got a little flour, sugar, and other condiments, made some cakes, and theefliture Sir Josiah turned out into the streets to sell the cakes, and so managed to subsist until something else turned up. You know the result; eventually he hit upon two in- ventions of an important character, and made himself a splendid fortune. He was connected with the electro- plating carried on under the firm of Elkington, Mason, and Co., manufacturers of steel pens. The Perry pen was really the invention of Sir Josiah Mason. He realised a great deal of money, and what did he do with it? He did not gamble it away as many do, nor spend it on his own private self, on luxury and extravagance, grand house building and so ; but he reserved for himself a very modest proportion, and the rest he devoted to the welfare of the public. The other one is President Garfield. (Applause.) I don't know that ever in the course of my reading I perused the history of a man with greater interest,—a history which is full of suggestion to the young of the present day. Young Gar- field began life as a bargee, and as the driver of a horse on the tow path of a canal. Can anybody imagine anything of a lower grade for a person to emerge from? Look at his career. The driver of a horse on one hand, and the presi- dent of a treat country on the other. And he accomplished it all by common tact and energy, not derogatory to the faculties of human nature. He was a God-fearing man from beginning to end, and of the highest possible intelligence. From a bargee he became a farm labourer, and then farmer himself. From that he took to study, and succeeded ad- mirably, in fact he did so in almost everything he under- took. lie became a professor at college, and from his pro- fessorship he offered his services as a soldier, and although he had not had anything to do with soldiering, he was most successful and was promoted to the rank of major-general, and contributed to win one of the decisive battles that put an end to the great war in America. From that he was re- commended by President Lincoln to leave the army and take his place ire Congress. Ho did •so as senator, and by his eloquence, right principle, and sagacity rose to the very first place in the assembly of the nation. I have not yet mentioned the whole of his qualifications. He was a very earnest preacher, and in that way was instrumental in pro- moting the welfare of his fellow countrymen. As an orator he succeeded admirably. I had the pleasure of reading one of his speeches which struck me as remarkable for sound sense and eloquent language. It may be said we cannot all be President Garfields or Sir Josiah Masons; but we can all act upon principles by which they were guided; and direct the use of our facullies to the best and wisest ends. Take the motto which will lead to successful life, aptitude and principle, and as Garfield put it—intention, attention, and intensity. We should have a high ideal, and prosecute that ideal with industry, effort, and never-tiring zeal, and afterwards be reading, as these two men of whom I have been speaking; and if we cannot succeed as they did, we venture upon a trial of a similar career-elf we do not get to the highest point we can at all events attain a very respectable position in life, and the young men I recommend to follow in their way. There is a little anecdote of Lord Nelson's promptitude, activity, and energy. When about to sail on his last voyage, which ended in the victory of Trafalgar to which he fell a sacrifice, he wanted certain articles sending to his ship, and he called upon a tradesman to order them. •" Now," he says, "I must have them sent down to my ship at such a time." "Oh, yes, by that time," was the reply. He looked at him and saw something like indecision in his countenance, and then said, 'Mr. Jones, a quarter of an hour before the time, it you please." "Oh, yes, my lord, a quarter of an hour before the time." "To that quarter of an hour," said Lord Nelson, "I owe everything I have in the world." I don't' know anything that contributes more to a man's failure than procrastination, and the want of punctuality. If a young man wishes to succeed in life he must have promptitude; decision, and punctuality. (Applause.) I am a great

div.p: 1 believer in the old fashioned principle of "Fear God and i honour Him." We live in a sceptical age. Ido not fear ' scepticism. I du not fear the fullest possible inquiry into any subject that can occepy the human mind. The mai ! who has the fear of God before his eyes has a far better chance of success iu the world than the man who has not— (applause)—and this is manifested most distinctly in the lives of those two men to whom I have called attention. I think I have said quite as much as I ought. Perhaps I have. detained you too long. I have had very great pleasure in attending this meeting to-night. It gives great promise of success. I congratulate my worthy friends, and Ih, -le 'they will be encouraged by the success hitherto, and not to slacken their labours, but persevere until these classes shall be recognised as superior—certainly not inferior—to any within the county. (Applause.) Major PILKINFON, who was received with cheers, had pleasure in rising to move "That the best thanks of this meeting he given to Sir James Picton for coming here this evening." (Cheers.) He was sure they welcomed him very heartily as one who knew something about them, having been connected with them, and taken considerable interest :n what had been going on in St. Helips. Sir James had not flattered them, but had told them exactly what he had thought about them. Speaking about buildings, he thought Sir James anew as much as most men about them, and if Sir James went round St. Helens he (the speaker) would be bound to say that there were to be found as well-built chimneys as they might wish to see. (Laughter.) He hoped the day was coming when there would be less smoke. Although he believed science could accomplish a great deal, he did not believe in the story that Sir William Thompson could sink a shaft and fix a wheel at the falls of Niagara lair run every mortal thing. That was very ridiculous, bat there was no doubt that electricity would play a muple I greater part in every department than it had done hitherto. He believed there was a prize for a lady that evening. Ile wished she had had the pluck to come and take It for her- self, as it would have incited other ladies to follow her example. He thought they had made quite enough of science in St. Helens. It was all very well to be working by the aid of science; but he did not believe in one con- tinual working. He believed in recreation, and he was glad to see at the other end of the room some signstof art. (Cheers.) It would be a good thing indeed if the young women of St. Helens would take up a little more art, for after the husband had been driving away at work all day he could go home at night, read a bit while his wife painted, or vice versa. It might become a very useful thing indeed. If the young fellow was laid up the wife would find painting much better than stitching or work of a similar character. He hoped the day would come when they would have a school of art in St. Helens; and they would be all the better for the enterprise. (Applause). The Rev. Canon CARR seconded the resolution, and said he had listened with intense interest to every word that fell from Sir James' lips. He had never heard him on such an occasion as that, but he hoped very much to have.the pleasure of hearing him again. There was one sentiment that he uttered which especially pleased him, and that was the union between science and religion. He believed science was the handmaid of religion, and he believed that no system of religion which did not embrace the progress of science was founded on truth. He felt indebted to Sir James for the many things he had told them about their darn town. He had told them many things he (the speaker) did not know bsfore. Alluding to the Cowley Hill middle. class schools, Canon Carr said he was ashamed that they should be standing still for the paltry sum 'nf a thousand pounds, for it was paltry compared to the wealth of St. Helens. But Sir James would excuse him when he said they did not require £l,OOO, but only £BOO. He had ex- perienced the liberality of the St. Helene people, and he could not believe that it would be allowell to stand still another month. If the-re could be found 39 persons to con- tribute £2O each, he would most heartily make up the fortieth person. He seconded most heartily the vote of thanks to Sir James Picton. _
Sir Jaws briefly responded, and the meeting terminated.

FDDISBURY PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before S. Wodebouse. Esq. (in the chair). G. F. Wilbraham, J. Higson, A. E. Wright, James Tomkinson, and W. Foster, Esqrs. Arrouvratzwr or A CLERIC.—The Chairman said in ct nr sequence of the dectase of Mr. Wm. Wood Blake, the late clerk to the magistrates, it became necessary for them to appoint a successor, and inasmuch as Mr. Rogers was leav- ing the firm, proposed that Mr. John Leigh Trafford should be ippointed to the office. At the same time they regretted that Mr. Rogers, who had been connected with them for so many years, was about to leave. The magistrates also wished to express their feelirg of satisfaction at the way in which he had conducted the work during the time he had held office.—Mr. Higson stated that he should be very glad indeed to second the proposition. Ile felt great satisfaction indeed at the way in which Mr. Rogers had conducted the business of the second court.—The proposition was con- firmed.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—EIizabeth Taylor, hawker, Frodsham, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly in Church-street, Frodsham.--John Taylor and. James Ainsworth, for being drunk and disorderly in Main- street, Frodsham, were fined, Taylor ss. and costs, and king: worth 10s, and costs..
KnEpurn • Dos wimour • LICENSE. - George Bryan was fined ss. and costs for keeping a dog without a license at Frodsham.

I ALLEGED ASSAULT BY VOLUNTEERS.—RaIph Lloyd and ' George Edge, two members of the Frodsbam volunteers, were summoned for assaulting George Lanceley, on land in the occupation of Mr. Watford, at Frodsham, on the 3rd of September.—Mr. Fletcher appeared for tha complainant Lancely.—lt appeared that for some time past the volun- teers had been in the habit of using the ground as a range. From a letter written to Lancely by Mr. lira!ford, as occu- pier of the land, and in whose employ he was, he communi- cated with the officer of the regiment concerning the matter' of the use of the ground. Captain Ashton said he was quite ready to make arrangements for the renting of the land if Mr. Watford objected to their using it without. But nothing was however done. On the 3rd September witness Went down to the range and told the volunteers they must not fire, when by the orders of the Sergeant-Instructor, they removed him from the ground.--Sergeant-Instrucctor Flannigan said the complainant used very violent language and threatened to use a stick he was carrying. Ile finally went and sat down in front of the target, when witness gave him three minutes to get away, if not he would be removed. Complainant did not go. and the two defendants were then instructed to remove him.—Captain Robert Ashton stated the corps had a right to the range given by the late Marquis. of Cholmondeley.—By Mr. Fletcher: Mr. Watford had told him he required £l5 a year for the use of the range, bat he had refused, and of ered £5 a year, which Mr. Watford bad. declined. The corps had had possession of the range for many years.—The matter was adjourned until the next meeting, in the hope that some arrangetnent might be made.

ASSAIILT.—Wm. Okell and Henry Walker were summoned for assaulting a man named James Hunt, at Kingslev.—lt appeared that complainant had occasion to go along the road on the Sunday afternoon in question, when he met the de- fendants and some other young men. For some reason or other (be beimr an Irishman and they Englishmen) they-set upon him. Walker kicked him in the back, and the other man threw a stone, which struck complainant on the head and inflicted such injuries that he was kept from work four days.—Okell, who was the only defendant who appeared, in consequence of some mistake in the name, stated that he was not the man who inflicted the injariem; men named Edward Robinson and Wm. Morton were, it was stated, the guilty parties, and on the suggestion of the Bench the charge against the defendants was withdrawn. DESERTING WIFE AND FAMILY.—Thomas Hamlett, Over, bricklayer, was charged with deserting his wife and two children, and leaving them chargeable to the Union— Mr. Fletcher appeared on behalf of the Northwich Guardians, and stated that the man was brought up on a warrant in September, 1879, when the magistrates dismissed the case on prisoner promising to pay a certain sum per week. That sum, had not been paid.—Arthur Arrowsmith, relieving officer, having been called in support of the case, the pri- soner in defence, questioned the moral character of the wife. —The Bench, disregarding the statement, he was sent or a month's imprisonment. CEVELTT TO 'A HORSE.—David Aston, Frodiharn, was charged by Inspector Demond Harper, of the R.5.P.0.A., for having, on the 12th tilt., used a cob which was not fit to go in harness. Wounds the size of a crown and a half- crown were on the body of the animal, which was in a bad state.—A fine of 10s. and costs was inflicted.

are well worthy of being carefully read and cond sidered by every working man in this populous district. He pointed out that the study of science by a people that was dependent more or less upon such trades as the smelting of copper, the manufactura of glass, and the making of alkali, was very important. We regard it as being of so much importance to the industrial and commercial community of this country that no pains ought to be spared to stimulate our artizans in this direction. A thorough technical education is absolutely necessary before the know- ledge which scientific men have obtained for us can be utilised by each particular trade or manufacture. Those who have watched the vast changes that have been brought about of late years in various branches of industry by the introduction of new machinery and the application of science to industrial operations see very plainly that we must not be content to tread in the footsteps of our forefathers; but that if Eng- land is to hold her own in the commercial world our working classes must apply themselves to the study of practical science. We have now a good Education Act in operation, under which every child is com- pelled to receive a sound elementary education. There is no excuse, therefore, for that condition of utter ignorance which in former years swelled the ranks of criminals and paupers, but we can only regard the elementary knowledge given in our day schools as the foundation upon which to rest something higher. We may rely upon it that the time will shortly come when we shall recognise the importance of seeing ' that this is supplemented by technical instruction which will enable our artizansto compete successfully with those of any other nation on the face of the globe. It is said that a German tofu has been suc- cessful in taking away a certain trade from one of our English towns, and that it is slowly undermining another in the same town. A writer, who has resided in both these towns, states that neither in physique nor in natural ability and energy are the foreigners equal to Englishmen. There is little doubt that as a race we have advantages in this respect, and yet our less qualified neighbours are per- mitted to compete with and outstrip us in the markets of the world. How is this? The answer is partly to be found in the educational advantages which Germany possesses and the readiness with which her workmen have availed themselves of the facilities afforded them for acquiring technical knowledge. Are the working men of England content to be beaten by men who are acknowledged to be weaker than them- selves ? We believe not, and therefore it is that we heartily coincide with Sir James Picton in pressing upon our working classes the necessity of applying themselves to the acquisition of scientific knowledge' The wonderful discoveries and the rapid advancement in science made in our own country in recent years are sufficient proof that there is no reason why those who have to depend upon copper, glass, and alkali works, should be content to drag out a weary existence amid columns of dense black smoke and in an at- mosphere filled with noxious vapours. We feel cer- tain that we have only to apply ourselves earnestly to scientific studies and researches in order to discover some means whereby the fumes, which at present are destructive to vegetable and animal life, may be profitably utilised, and at the same time rendered to a great extent innocuous. The report read on Friday night shows that the studies of the science and art classes include a variety of useful subjects which have a direct bearing upon our manufactures. Whilst, therefore, we con- gratulate the committee on the success whieh has a afforded attended their efforts, we feel that it is impossible to i our opportunitiesrnepnressf ur manufacturing too strongly upon the minds of the working m towns them t he o importance acquiring af seizing the thorough knowledge of applied science in at least the branches peculiarly interesting to them.

MT. PIERS EGERTON WARBITRTON, M.P., responding to the toast of "The County Members" at the Altrincham Agricultural Show on Thursday, told the Cheshire farmers that the last session of Parliament had been one of the longest, and "to his mind one of the most, profitless sessions on record, for he could not say that that there had been a single measure passed of any benefit either to Englishmen or Scotchmen, and he was not quite cqrtain whether the session had been of any benefit even to Irishmen." Summing up the work of the session, he said that two measures had been undertaken. " First, the Irish Land Bill—a very bad bill—had been carried through the House; and, secondly, Mr. Bradlaugh—a very .bad man—had been carried out." Mr. Warburton may be regarded as an authority in politics by those who do not know any better; but we happen to differ from the bon. gentleman as to the value of the work done during the last session, and we believe that the majority of Englishmen and Scotchrnen also regard the Irish Land Bill as a measure of justice to their fellow•countrymen in Ireland. The old school of Conservatives to which Mr. Warburton evidently belongs have ever been ready to promise to do every- thing they could for the agriculturists in order to secure their suffrages, and we wore not surprised to learn that Mr. Warbarton;had given just such a promise to the farmers of Cheshire. Mr. War- burton sympathises so very deeply with the Cheshire farmers that he expresses himself ready to support any measure for their benefit. He, however, fears now agriculture is in such a sad state, and seeing that the Irish people have just had a Land Act, that the English farmers will shortly follow suit and demand an alteration in the land laws of this country, and so whilst he tells the agriculturists that he will vote for any measure for their benefit, he does not hesitate to disparage the Irish Land Act by calling it a very bad "bill, and the session which passed it a profitless .one. It is more than probable, however, that English farmers will examine this question for themselves, and when they find, as they will do, that the land laws of this coun- try tend to grind them down they will unite together in demanding that their grievances shall be redressed and that those who promisely so fairly shall show by their actions that they really mean what they say.

- Mr. the district, ia e superintendent afondness ing t amounting rforo nearlyßun corn and ha monomania for red-tapeism and sections of A Board, f l ment, has written to the Local Government com- plaining that Dr. McDougall, when en a brief holiday, some short time ago, had not himself signed the vaccination papers but had employed a deputy to do so. This seems to o Parlia- ment, ia- have offended the righteous soul of Mr. Coleburn, who ap- parently went out of his way to direct the attention of the Board in London to the conduct of the doctor. The matter was ultimately brought before the Runcorn Board of Guardians, and the clerk (Mr. Henry Linaker) held that Dr. McDougall was perfectly justified, under his contract, in appointing a deputy whilst he was away. Mr. Thomas Norman and Mr. William Handley also remarked that they were of opinion Mr. Coleburn had been over-officious in the matter. Unfortunately, there are a good many people in this wicked world who have a similar inclination. Perhaps Mr. Coleburn will try what a little courtesy will do in the nf uo ttubr when be quite dealing so fond with b ani officialngoff whatever be af t et uh eet littleG u ar daiva authority raintyd he may possess. From the opinions expressed by the two guardians It would appear as if he had the bump of self- esteem rather abnormally developed.

The party on the Widnes Board who are opposed to the holding of the fair is growing stronger, and it seems highly probable that the fate of the saturnalia is nearly sealed. This year the motion to advertise the holding of it was only carried by the casting vote of the chairman.

The committee of the Farnworth Agricultural Show were, onithe first day of their exhibition, favoured with lovely weather, and they cannot have had a very bad day eveli on the Saturday. I, nevertheless, bear that the pecuniary re- sult is not so large as to do anything towards reducing the debt. At the luncheon, which was honoured by a visit from an ex-cabinet mintster, and presided over by Mr. A. B. Walker, of Liverpool, Mr. Whalley, himself a farmer of the first class, made the somewhat depressing assertion that, tak- ing Lancashire and Cheshire through, not one third of the farmers were solvent. This says a great deal in favour of a reduction in rents, and a new Land Act for the farmers of this country. Let us hope that something will be done during the coming session to relieve the English farmers of their many burdens.

div.head: EX A_IIIINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 1, 1881.
div.p: THE EX A_IIIINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 1, 1881.

One is almost tired of reading anything about the finances of the Widnes Board, which have for several years either been considerably " mixed," or shown a balance at the wrong side of the ledger. The general public were hopeful that they had heard the last of the confusion when Mr. Allen took the helm as accountant, and latterly as clerk, but he seems to have had an Augean stable of finance to cleanse, and as he does not profess to be a second Hercules even in such a matter as accounts, the work of putting affairs to right only progresses at a moderate pace. For some time the accounts of the Highway Committee have been in an. almost inextricable tangle, owing to some one at the head of that body, in former years, not having had a proper know- ledge of when to charge an item of expenditure to capital and when to put it down to revenue account. So thick had the fog in which the accounts of this committee were some time ago involved become, that about £B,OOO was in ques- tion. Not that the money was missing, but it was not charged so as to obtain the sanction of the auditor to the Local Government Board. At the last meeting it was stated that the 91.1tVeyer had corrected the expenditure to the extent of £2,459 us. 3d., but the facts as to the rest of the sum were, up to that date, in Stygian darkness. Mr. Allen's duties cannot be exactly a bed of roses.

--- Runcornians must receive a considerable measure of gratification from the fact that the pictures of one of their townsmen—Mr. A. T. Nowell—are taking such a position in the world of art as to be considered worthy of a place in the Manchester and Liverpool exhibitions.

Mr. Rigby, one of the Guardians of the Runcorn Union, was somewhat blunt at the last meeting of that body when, in the presence of the vicar of the parish, who is also an honorary canon of Chester cathedral, he stated that the man who "invented " tithes ought to be put on the top of a pole and be burned. This is certainly very strong language, expressive of the disgust with which the farmers look upon this most unfair impost. There was a time when a similar expression of opinion would have caused Mr. Rigby to be ostracised by the whole country, but its utterance merely raised a laugh. - - -

The Parliamentary Debating Society at Runcorn, hold their opening soiree at the Public Hall next Friday. The officers and members of the "Poor Man's Friendly Burial Society " will by this time have learnt that although in past years the officers of friendly societies have iven allowed to neglect to comply with some of the provisions of the former Friendly Society Act with impunity, this state of things is not going to be continued. The present Act of Parliament is far more stringent in its provisions than the old one, and the Government officials appear resolved to carry them into operation with impartiality. Certain privi- leges are conferred upon those societies that comply with the provisions of the Ac' t and the violation of any clause will certainly be followed by the infliction of a penalty. The Poor Man's Friendly Burial Society, held at the White Horse Inn, Naylor-street, St. Helens, has violated the provi- sion of the Act with respect to the valuation of its assets and liabilities, and the result is that the Chief Registrar has now suspended the registry of the society for three months so that during that period it will Cease to enjoy the privileges of a registered society. This sentence of suspension will not prevent any one who has a legal claim against the so- ciety from enforcing it, but I do not think that it will tend to raise the society in the estimation of the public. Probably the publication of this decision on the part of the Chief Re- gistrar will prove a warning to other societies not to neglect to comply with the requirements of the Act of Parliament which has been passed in the interests of such societies. It is rumoured that a very respectable young gentleman, who is alleged to have broken his promises to more than one lady in this neighbourhood, is likely to have to appear as defendant in an action for breach of promise of marriage on account of his treatment of a beautiful young damsel to whom he has been paying assiduous attentions for some time past. This fair daughter of Eve is said to have taken the cruel desertion of her lover very much to heart, the re- sult being a very serious illness. To the joy of her friends and relatives the young lady, however, is now slowly but surely regaining her former good health, and if all I hear be true her inconstant swain will very soon learn the truth of the saying that "Heaven ha- no rage like love to hatred turned, Nor hell a fury like a woman scorned."

The lecture season is close upon us, and I hope that during the coming winter we shall find the Liberal Associations of this district arranging, by means of lectures and the dis- semination of reliable information, to educate the masses up to the great and urgently-needed measures of reform which were promised by the present Government when it came into power. No one doubts that Mr. Gladstone's Govern- ment will redeem its pledges; but the obstruction which the Government has met with in the House of Commons, the constant opposition of the House of Lords to all great popular measures, and the audacity with which a section of the Tory party has lately sought to beguile the constituencies from their allegiance to the traditional Free Trade principles of England, ali point to the urgent necessity of vigorous action on our part, both to counteract the mischiefs arising from these sources, and also to evoke that populat support without which even Mr. Gladstone and his powerful Government will be unable to carry to a successful issue the beneficent legislative schemes which they are known to have in view. It is therefore very important that each Liberal Association should be actively engaged in the pro- pagation of Liberal principles during the ensuing season. FLACCUS.

Rurrconw MEnsaY MrssroN.— On Monday evening, a second meeting for the season was held in connection with this mission. Mr. W. Cooper, bandmaster, presided. WIDNES FAlR.—This fair commenced on Thursday, and we understand, finishes to-day (Saturday.) The proceedings on the first day wesvery "flat, stale, and unprofitable." RUNCORN ELLESMERE-STREET IMTROVEMENT CLASS.-- Monday evening was the commencement of the winter session. Mr. John Holford, the president, occupied the chair, and about 40 members were present. Mr. Richard Moore is the secretary.

WIDNES SCiENCE AND ART CLASSES.—The annual dis- tribution of ptizes in connection with the Widnes Science and Art Classes, will take place on Tuesday evening, in the Volunteer Hall, by Dr. Oliver J. Lodge, of London. Mr. J. Brock will occupy the chair, and no doubt deliver an interesting address. The eighth session of the classes com- mences on Monday, the 3rd instant. RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.—It will be seen from our advertising columns that the com- mittee of this society have decided to start the session in a manner which will no doubt attract considerable attention to their proceedings. They intenEl to have a soirée in the Public Hall on Friday, the 6th inst., and tickets may be obtained from Mr. Thomas Handley, the Speaker, or Ntr. Rogerson.

REV. Doi. STEPHENSON, OF LONDON, TO VISIT RUN- coRN.—Mr. Stephenson, who ha o made for himself a name which will live amongst the annals of Wesleyan Methodism, when he has gone over to the great majority, will visit Run- corn on Wednesday, and in the evening the band and choir of the Children's Home, Orphanage and Refuge (London), will give a miscellaneous entertainment in the Public Hall. Great interest has always been taken in the noble work of Mr. Stephenson, in Runcorn, and there is certain to be a good attendance. STAR OF TEMPERANCE BRASS BAND, WIDNES.—This band will perform the following programme of music on the Promenade on Saturday, from 2.30 to 5 o'clock--March," The Wonder," George; overture, " Confidence," J. RUNCORN PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.-011 Tuesday evening a meeting of the members and friends o ther above society was held in Bethesda schoolroom, Run corn, Mr. Shore presiding. The Chairman said that at the meeting of the council lilst week it was thought desirable that a gathering of members and intending members should be called to decide whether another session should or should not be held. The feeling of the council seemed to be that, if after advertising, they could not get a sufficient number to join, so to form a better class than the one they had last session, the society had better be closed in a formal way. It would be an absurdity to have a parliament of only twenty or thirty members. The greater the number of members, and the more likely it would be that they would gain the end for which the association had been organised. After a prolonged discussion, it was decided that the session should be opened by holding a soiree in the Public Hall, for mem- bers of the society and their friends who intended joining the class.

Mr. F. Fairhurst presided. The same lady will preach at St. John's chapel, on Sunday evening. SHOCKING DEATH AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday an inquest was held at the Mersey Hotel, Widnes, before Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, on the body of John Walsh, who met his death by falling into a vat of chemi- cals. Mary Walsh, of 22,11igh-street, Widnes, said deceased was her husband and worked as a vatman at Messrs. Gaskell, Deakin and Co.'s chemical works. On Sunday, the 4th instant, he left-home at about five minutes past four in the afternoon, intending to finish the work on which he had been engaged and return home immediately. A short time afterwards she was informed that he had met with an acci- dent and been taken to the hospital, where she saw him the same evening. She had visited him at different times, and he had told her that the accident was owing to the plank over which he was wheeling being worn by the constant action of the wheel upon it. The barrow had capsized, and on his making an effort to right it had fallen into the vat, carrying him along with it. She last saw him alive on the Friday before the day of his death, which occurred on Sun- day, the 25th.—Barnard Grennan said he lived at 26, Eleanor-street, and worked at the same works as deceased. Walsh and himself were engaged on the day in question in wheeling black ash to some vats which contained chemi- cals. The barrow "run " consisted of three nine inch planks laid side by side and joined together by three iron rods. Immediately before the accident deceased had gone up the planks with his barrow loaded with black ash, and he (witness) was waiting with his barrow at the bottom of the hoist by which the barrows were lifted on to the planks. Hearing the noise of of the falling barrow, he turned round and SAW Patrick Dillon, another workman, reaching down apparently trying to pull the man out of the vat. Witness ran up to the spot, and taking hold of the flannel singlet which deceased wore he endeavoured to pull him out, but the flannel gave way and he fell in again. By the joint efforts of himself and Dillon they at last succeeded in getting deceased out by the cord, or rope. which he wore as a belt. They took him to a vat of weak liquor and there washed him and afterwards cleansed him with water. A lad was sent to the office for some oil with which they anointed deceased, and he was then taken to the hospi- tal in a cab, and on the way he was joined by Dr. McDon- nell, who attended him. Witness said that the planks were tolerably level and free from knots' and the only inequality in them was the groove made by the continual running of the wheel upon them. It was a thing of common occurrence to drop a lump of black ash off the barrows, and it wag his opinion that it was this that had caused the barrow to cap- size.—Patrick Dillon, of 4, Hope-street, deposed that he was a labourer, and worked at the same place as the de- ceased. On the 4th inst., between four and five o'clock, he was at the top of the stage, taking his vest and muffler off, previous to commencing work. Deceased passed him with his barrow, which he observed was not more heavily loaded than usual. Witness was in the act of hanging his vest up, when he heard the plunge of the barrow into the vat. He immediately tried to pull deceased by taking him by the arm, but was unable to do so. The previous witness came to his asaistance, and they then succeeded in getting him out. —The Coroner : Did you see anything on the plank that would be likely to throw the barrow wheel over ?—Witness: I saw a lump of black-ash off his barrow, which was quite sufficient to have thrown him over, if his wheel had struck it. There was a groove made by the barrow wheel, but otherwise the plank was in good condition. Deceased had been accustomed to the work, having wheeled over the same vats for a period extending over twelve months.—Mr. Mor- rison, who attended on behalf of the firm, laid before the jury a plan of the vats 'and the stage along_which the bar- rows had to run. He said the stage would be about two feet three inches wide, and he had heard no complaints shout the planks being badly worn. The men were paid ac- cording to the number of vats they filled, and they worked very rapidly in order to get a lot of work done. The jury I returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

ATHLETIC SPORTS AT ORFORD BAUR/XIS. -The monotonous routine of life in the barracks was considerably relieved on Thursday, when the annual athletic sports of the Bth and 40th regimental districts took place. The arrangements were under the direction of Colonel H. De R. Pigott., Major Nicholson, Major Whiffing, Captains Flood, Turnbull, and Chadwick, and a sub-committee composed of Sergeant-Majors McCarty, Cannon, Burns, Finnelly, and Chubb. Being favoured with beautiful weather, the events, which were very numerous, all passed off well, the various competitions being on the whole well contested. Several of the races were open to volunteers of the district. The highest prize was 303., the majority, however, ranging from 15s. to is; The judges were Colonel H. Der R. Pigott, Major Whitting, and Major Nicholson, and their decisions were uni- versally satisfactory. The following is the prize list :-High jump: Ist, Private Guilfoyle, South Lancashire Regiment; 2, Private Jones, Liverpool Regiment. Putting the shot (32ibs.) without follow: Ist, Private Stone, South Lancashire Regi- ment ; 2nd, Sergeant Logan, 3rd battalion. The winning throw was 21 feet. Running long jump: Ist, Lance-Corporal Dickinson; 2nd, Lance-Corporal Stacey, both of the Liver- pool Regiment. Flat race, round the course, for non-com- missioned officers: let, Lance-Cerporal Courtney, South Lancashire Regiment; 2nd, Sergeant Friar, 3rd battalion; 3rd, Lance-Corporal Leonard, 3rd battalion. Flat race, 440 yards: Ist, Private Holland; 2nd, Private Webster; 3rd, Drummer Jolley, all of the South Lancashire Regi- ment. Flat race, 100 yards. for children of non-commissioned officers and men of the Bth and 40th regimental districts: Ist, Fox ; 2nd, Regan ; 3rd, Matchett. Heavy marching order race, round the course :-Ist, P irate Holland, South Lancashire; 2nd, Private Stone. In this race the competitors, of whom there were five, were fully accoutred, which made it extremely laborious to run. Flat race; 880 yards :-Ist, Private Holland ; 2nd, Private Bourne, Ist Battalion; 3rd, Drummer Jolley. Flat race, round the course :-Ist, Private Hough; 2nd, Private Doglass ; 3rd, Barnes, all of the South Lanca- shire Regiment. Veterans' race, round the course, for non- commissioned officers and men over 16 years' service :-Ist, Private Matchett; 2nd, Sergeant Friar; 3rd, Sergeant Wilson. Flat race, 880 yards (open to volunteers):-18t, Private Barnes, 9th Lancashire Volunteers; 2nd, Private Walsh, 4th King's Own; 3rd, Bough, 9th Lancashire Volunteers. Tug of war, eight men a side Bth Regimental District v. the 40th. Only one pull was allowed, and after a most stubborn struggle the 40th had to submit. Colonel Pigott then offered another prize of £l, the tug to be decided in three pulls. The first one was a steady pull, but eventually the Bth Regiment's team, which contained the smallest men, pulled their opponents over the line. When the second pull was called for the men of the 40th refused, to come forward, and acknowledged themselves beaten. Three-legged race-let, Private Matchett and Corporal Leonard; 2nd, Lance-Corporals Stacey and Sephton ; 3rd, Lance-Corporal Craig and Private Dalev. Flat race, 100 yarda (open to volunteers) :-Ist, Private Walsh ; 2nd, Private Slater, 9th Lancashire Volunteers. Bucket race ' (blindfold) :-let, Private Guilfovl e ;2nd, Private Richmond ! Monkey race: let, Private McGrath; 2nd, Private Healey; 3rd, Private Wallace. One mile flat race (open to volunteers): I let (305.) Private Barnes; 2nd (155.) Private Rough; 3rd ' (10s.) Private Clara; all of the 9th Lancashire Volunteers. Sack race; Ist, Private McGrath ; 2nd, Private Guilfoyle. Clog dancing: let, Private Gallagher, Liverpool regiment; 2nd, divided between Privates McDonald and Lea, 4th King's own. Officers' servants' race: Ist, Stone; 2nd, Meredith ; 3rd, Stanley. Consolation race round the course, for all beaten competitors of the depots: Ist, Private Gilroy, South Lancashire ; 2nd, Private Arnold, Liverpool. There were no entries for the tumbling competition, but Private Lister showed Some extraordinary balancing fe,ats. He fixed upon the end of a gun, a sword, the point of which be placed upon his chin, balancing it with the utmost ease. He also balanced a couple of ordinary heavy wood forms, placed in the shape of a cross, upon his chin, and a square board the size of an ordinary table. The spectators loudly applauded. During the afternoon the bands of the 2nd and 4th King's Own regiment discoursed some excellent music. AN PISODE OF THE Butram Aer. Two or three days ago a gentleman in Preston, who had embraced the Unitarian belief, was interred in the cemetery of that town under rather unpleasant circumstances. rhe relatives of the deceased desired to inter his remains in the Church of England portion of the ground, but when they arrived at the cemetery they were told by the sexton that as the notice of interment there had not arrived within the time prescribed by the Act, the corpse must be interred with the burial ser- vice of the Established Church. Rather than run the risk of a " scene " at that solemn moment, the relatives of the deceased complied with the course laid down by the sexton. ME. GLADSTONE AND THE NONCONFORMISTS. —Mr. Gladstone has just replied to a correspondent who called his attention to a charge brought against him by a Yorkshire Conservative paper that he had recommended that Noncon- formists should be excluded from all civil offices. The charge was connected with a quotation from Mr. Gladstone's work', " The State in its relations with the Church." The reply of the Premier is as follows:—"10, Downing-street, el.all. Sept. Sir,—Mr. Gladstone desires me act rhwkilge the recript of your note enclosing an extract, which it appears to be iuleurd that in his book called rile State in its relations with the Church " he recom- mended the exclusion of Nonconformists from all civil olllees; and, in reply, I am to ohserve that there is no citation to suppiu t such a charge, which he believes to lor groundless.- 1 am, str. your oba client servant. E. W. HAMILTON."

Tun COTTON COBNER.—The six days stoppage of niills in this county in order to defeat in soma measure the Liverpool "corner" is stated to have effected over twelve million spindles. Three million spindles were kept at work. At Bacup on Tuesday a numerously attended meeting of employers agreed to stop their mills for another six days if such a proceeding were sanctioned by the next general meet- ing to be held in Manchester. The loss in wages in Oldham alone now amounts to many thousands of pounds.—At an adjourned meeting on Tuesday, at Manchester, of Yorkshire cotton spinners, in reference to the Liverpool "cotton corner," it was resolved to work four days a week for a month. The replies so far received by Mr. Guthrie, the 13ecretary of the Cotton Spinners' Association, to his circular inquiring whether spinners are prepared to stop their mills for a farther period, are with few exceptions in favour of stoppage of work for another week.

RON ON A CO -OPERATIVE SOCIETY.-011 Saturday, owing to certain rumours respecting the Leigh Friendly Co- operative Society., a number of members went to withdraw their investments or to give notice of withdrawal. Not more than £3 is payable on application. The report for the March quarter gives the number of members as 3,282, and the sales in the grocery and provision department £16,881, of which £2,483 was disposable profit; and after paying £Bl2 for interest on members shares, .£96 for depreciation of fixed stock, and £l9 for educational purposes, a dividend of is. 91 in the pound was declared. Besides clog and shoe, drapery, tailoring, and butchering departments, there are 13 branch shops in addition to the central store. The society has also a corn mill and a manufacturing department. Re- specting the latter, the March half-yearly reports represents the share, account at £32,000; and against this, in the capital account, buildings represent £6,488; mill gearing, £3,089; machinery, £5,942; stock-in-trade, £14,663; cash in band, £1,526; and balance, £238. ENFORCED CELIB&CY AMONG THE CHESHIRE POLICE. —Before the magisterial business commenced on Thursday at Nantwich Police Court, Mr. Wilbraham Tollemache stated the case of a man who had applied to him for a re- 'commendation to enter tne police force. Ile told him to go to the superintendent at Nantwich, Mr. Mayho, and, to his (Mr. Tollemache's) surprise, a printed form was produced setting forth that no constable was allowed to marry. Un- fortunately, the man hi question was a married man. He considered that a policeman had as much right to a comfort- able home and the society of his wife as other men. He supposed policemen were open to the blandishments of the fair sex as well as other people. It was the first time he had heard of this order, or he should have brought it up before the Police Committee. He hoped that the new chief con- stable would alter the order, as it certainly did not conduce to morality. It was like the Zulu custom of not permitting a man to marry till he had performed some warlike service. It was pointed ont to Mr. Tollemache that the prohibition only extenled to three years on constables joining the force, and the magistrate said he considered the order a monstrous one.

FURTHER DISCOVERY OF BRINE SPRINGS IN CHESHIRE. —A good deal of interest has been excited in Cheshire during the past week by the tapping of some brine springs at Nantwich, in connection w;th a sanatorium and salt bath scheme. The operation of sinking for the brine was entrusted to Messrs. Bayley and Son, of Salford, and boring was commenced in a garden attached to Parkfield. After reaching a depth of 17ft. the point of the boring rod came in contact with a stratum of steel marl. This layer was penetrated to a depth of ten feet, but the experiment had to be abandoned in consequence of the strong deposits below. Operati6ns were afterwards directed from another spot. Boring to a depth of 19 feet, the steel marl and hard flag I were again en,:ountered, and after passing into it for some distance the brine came flowing up freely through the boring pipes. Further experiments show that there is salt in abundance, although at present only the surface of the brine stream has been tapped.

SI2fGI7LIII SCENE AT A. TEA PAnTY. —An Ashton correspondent writes to the Wigan Observer as follows : On Monday evening last, a somewhat unusual incident oc- curred at Ashton-in-Makerfield. It appears that a Sick and Burial Society in connection with St. Thomas's schools wto celebrating its annual tea party and dance in the schools above-named, when the Vicar noticed among the assembled devotees of terpsichorean art, a young man whom he recog- nised as one of those wicked (?) people who sit down in church during the singing of certain hymns. The partici- pition in, and apparent enjoyment of the evening's pleasures provided for the public on the payment of a stipulated fee, was more than the rev, gentleman's indignation could po3- sibly bear, and after a short space of time, approaching the young man he quietly informed him that "he (the vicar) could not allow him to remain there," and in reply to the interrogation "for what reason ?" he said, "because you annoy the congregation by sitting down at the singing of certain hymns in church." The young man's request for the return of the fee paid on admission was acceded to by the vicar, whe took the opportunity of reiterating his rea- sons for this expulsion from a public assembly. Remarks on this exhibition of clerical autocracy are needless.

MINERS' WAGES IN LANCASHIRE.—APPLICATION FOR AN ADVANCE —The following notice issued by the Lanca- shire Miners' Federation was forwarded on Monday to the colliery proprietors in Lancashire :—"Gentlemen,—At a conference of Lancashire miners, held September 24th, 1881, it was resolved unanimously to give yo a 14 days' notice for an advance in wages of 15 per cent., nooice to expire October 12th. We need not remind you that 12 moaths ago We solicited you for an advance, but failed to obtain our request. Towards the end of the year we demanded an advance. Thousands of miners in Lancashire received an advance in their wages in December last; others in January, February, and March in this year, but (with few exceptions) the wages of these miners are as low, and in some cases lower, than they were twelve months ago. We seed not inform you, because you know already, that our wages are far too low. Our labour is sold at the expense of half-clad wives and children, and very often half-filled stomachs. We believe your position to be bad, but you have never experienced the above, therefore ours is considerably worse. The greatly improvsd state of the coal trade, we believe, fully justifies us in our request for an advance in wages. A deputation of your miners will wait upon you on the sth day of October, or any other date to suit your con- nience, previous to the Bth.—Hoping we shall be able to I settle matters peaceably, we remain, yours truly, THE MINERS IN YOUR EMPLOY.

RELIGION AND POLITICS. —The Rev. R. P. Cook, who is leaving the pastorate of the Baptist denomination at Nantwich, after ten years' service, was on Tnesday pre- sented with a purse of gold, and the opportunity was taken to thank him for the services he rendered to the Liberal patty during the late contest in West Cheshire.—Mr. Jones said that no doubt the reverend gentleman had given offence in some quarters by his hearty and persistent advocacy of the Liberal cause; but, feeling that certain principles were true and right, he had done his utmost to enforce them upon the people. They needed sound political education in towns like Nantwich, and ministers needed no apology for in- structing them in the subject. Clergymen who did not study politics really left out half of the world's work. Every minister should be a thorough politician, and thus qualify' himself for instructing and directing his people aright in matters social and political, as well as religious. Several others addressed the meeting. The Rev. Mr. Cook, in reply, said that when he became a minister of the gospel he did not cease to be a citizen of the realm, nor !did it debar him from exercising his secular rights. Some time ago, in the heat of political excitement, it seemed to some people a very strange sight to find a minister of religion come to the front on a great occasion such as that was. But he offered no apology for his conduct. If he had to cease to be a man in order to become a minicer, he would cease to be a minister, and become a man again. (Applause.) As a Christian he owed a duty to the State, and he regarded it as one of the highest responsibilities laid upon bins that he I 9hould discharge that duty as a citizen of the realm in the fear of God and for the benefit of his fellow-men.

ATTEMPTED SUICIDE BY A HALTON FARM LABOURER. On the evening of the 23rd ult., Michael Duffy, a labourer, employed at Mr. John Ackerley's farm, Astmoor Bridge, near Halton, tried to commit suicide insthe straw shed by cutting his throat. Some of his fellow-workmen caught him in the act, and prevented his proceeding further. Dr. Carruthers was sent for, and is now attending the poor man, who has been suffering from depression of spirits. ST. HFLENS STARE-BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETIL—Tbe 4th appropriation meeting of this society was held in the:Market Tavern Cocoa Rooms, on Wednes- day, Mr. Henry Barr in the chair. Previous to the appropriation being made the secretary (Mr. Griffin) reported that the society then numbered 332 members holding over 750 shares. After the minutes of the previous meeting had been read, Messrs. Woodcock and Blackleelge were appointed to act as, Scrutineers, and a boy chosen to draw the ballot balls. The ballot resulted in No. 97 being drawn in. After this had been confirmed by resolution the successful member was announced to be Miss Frances Chadwick Croppers Hill, ten years of age, who having one share, becomes entitled to £lOO without interest for 12i years. The successful member is the daughter of Mr. Chadwick, who won the last appropriation. THRIFT IN Bemoan:ca.—Mr. A. Belgrave, Chief In- spector of Factories, has issued the following circular to occupiers of factories :—" You are doubtless aware of the plans which have been recently instituted by the Post Office authorities for increasing the opportunities and facilities by which money may be deposited in the Post Office Savings' I Bank. Mr. Fawcett, Her Majesty's Postmaster-General, has described the various proposals in his pamphlet 'Aids to Thrift,' copies of which are to be obtained fro n all post offices. But it appears to be very desirable to make knows as widely as possibly how tho Brst step in the lesson of economy may be taken, and this it is particularly essential to inculcate upon the younger members of a family, who are earning wages, and have some portion, however small it nrly be, given to them for their own use. The enclosed notice has been drawn up in the hope that you will permit I it to be affixed in some part of your factory where it may be read by your workpeople. It has been suggested that where it meets with the approval of the principals, one of the over- lookers, or persons in authority, might be permitted by them to receive the postage stamp forms when filled up by the children or young persons, and to obtain the accaunt books for them, so as to give the young a helping hand and a start in the early practice'of economy."—The "notice" mentioned in the circular is a small placard explaining the recent scheme for saving small sums by depositing postage stamps in the post office, and showing how accounts can be opened, and ultimately a depositor can become a purchaser of Government stock.

WonxrpromtN's MISSION, BANK QUAY.—On Sunday last the anniversary sermons in connection with the above place were preached, in the morning, by the Rev. T. Brewt- nall, of Didsbury College, who officiated in the absence through sickness, of the Rev. F. S. Hagen. The rev, gentle- man grounded his discourse upon the 2 Cor., v., 14, from which he preached a most eloquent sermon, which was thoroughly enjoyed by his hearers. In the afternoon Mr. Richard Johnson, of Manchester, conducted a children's ser- vice in the Bold-street Chapel, which was kindly lent for the occasion. Mr. Johnson spoke very effectively to a large I audience from the words "Be sure your sins will find you, out." His illustrations moved the people very much, and all were highly interested. The evening service was the crowning one, as we never remember seeing so large a num- ber of people assembled, or rather packed, in the chapel. Long before the time appointed every available inch of room was taken, porch and aisle being crammed with people eager to see and hear, and the outside presented an appear- ance still more remarkable, the space in front of the chapel right up to the steps being filled with people wishing to get in, one good friend going so far as to say he would give a half-crown if he could but get in, even if he had to stand up. Large numbers had to go away, and the opinion was freely expressed that whilst the chapel might do for the or- dinary services, it meet certainly is not large enough for special occasions. Mr. Johnson preached from Galatians vi.,2. Mr. Johnson has had a wide experienca, in Sunday school work, possesses a very fluent and distinct delivery, a rich store of illustration, and therefore,our readers can easily un- derstand that his audience were much interested, and it is hoped that good results will follow. During the morning ' and evening service the children, the le Icl.rsl:ip of Mr F. Willi uns. sang a selection of hymns in a ni inner which won the Tra4e. of All, and rellocied the 4.4'4 on the condtvt.w. the children were neat and dealt and their happy faces inn=t have pleased their teachers Ind friends. These services are said to have been in every respect the greatest success ever seen at Bank Quay. The collections morning and evening amounted to £l9 7s 3d, and in the afternoon £lO 2s sd, making a total of £29 95 8d; almost double the amount of coy other year.
