YOB FRODSRAM.—A pnblic meeting was held in the Girl's School, on Tuesday evening, to con- sider the desirability of forming a musical society for Frod- sham, when the vicar, the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., presided. A long discussion took place, and on the motion of the Vicar, st.conded by Mr. Charles E. Linaker, the following com- mittee was appointed to obtain information, and the names of intending members :—Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., Messrs. Chas. Reynolds, J. Bolderstone, H. G. Linaker, W. Cameron, Thomas Riley, Peter Riley, Henry Tiley, E. P. Dignum, A. Jones P. Nickson. and John S. Rimmer. _ _

LECTURE BY MISS !Meld=lnE.—On Tuesday evening a lecture was given in the ToWn Hall. Frodshans, by Miss McLatchie, on the subject of "Cromwell, the Puritans, and the English Martyrs," who delivered an eloquent impressive discourse. The Rev. F. F. Edmunds presided, and there was a large and appreciative audience. The usual vote of thanks to Miss McLatchie and the Chairman, brought the proceed- ings to a close.

STINDAY SCHOOL AWNIVERSARY.—The annual sermons in connection with the Union Church Sun,lay School, Sutton Weaver, were preached on Sunday, by the Rev. W. Elmslie, of Liverpool. A special selection of hymns was given by the scholars and a collection was made at the close of each service in aid of the funds of the Sunday school. THE PARISH CHURCH RESTORATION BAZAAR.—The ac- counts in connection with the above bazaar, were submitted to the committee on Wednesday-evening, from which it ap- peared that the net proceeds, after discharging all expenses, amounted to the handsome LIM of £BlO 14s. ed., and a con- siderable addition is hoped to be made by the sale of goods left over from the bazaar. It was resolved to hand the aoove sum forthwith to the Church Restoration Committee.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COU!tT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Bibby (chairman) and Mr. F. H. Gossage.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COU!tT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Bibby (chairman) and Mr. F. H. Gossage.

FEAUDELF.NT REMOVAL or GOODS. —Robert Stanton, a middle aged man, was charged with having fraudulently removed goods from the house of Mrs. Jane Sadler, Carlile- street, on tne 12th inst., with intent to avoid payment of rent. Complainant said that defendant owed her £2, and in the course cf the night he took away most of his furniture.— Defendant now said that the dwelling was not fit to live in as water came through the roof.—The Bench ordered him to pay 10s. on Saturday, and the rest of the amount at 2s. per week, and in default of so doing said be would be brought up again.

BREAKING OPEN A STABLE: HEAVY FINE.—Wm. Dwyer was charged with doing damage to the amount of 58. to a stable, the property of Mr. Wm. Higginson, farmer.—Com- plainant stated that he had been much troubled by two horses &longing to Dwyer going into his fields. He had spoken to the defendant four times about the nuisance, but he appeared to take no notice, for on the 16th inst., he found the animals there again. He took them to his stable and fastened them up. Sometime afterwards defendant came on the premises, broke off the stable lock and damaged the door. —Defendant said he had offered complainant 2s. 6d: to take the horses out.—The Chairman said it would have made no difference if he had offered a sovereign.—A witness was called for the defence, who said he examined the door the morning after the alleged damage was said to have been committed, and there was nothing amiss with it. —Defendant was fined 20e. and costs, and ss. damages, Or, in default of Payment, ordered to be sent to gaol one month, with bard labour.

STEALING SCRAP-IRON.—James Taylor, Michael John Keegan, an Simon Kilroy, all boys, were charged with stealing Scrap-iron; value -Is. Sd., the property of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Co.—Mr. Itichity4 Bayley appeared for the firm, and said that on the 19thsinst., about ten o'clock in the morning, he went to a shed in the yard, where there were from 100 to 120 iron bands. On the 22nd inst., he found that all the bands were gone.--P.C. Ross said that on Thursday last he was on duty on the canal bank, near to the firm's works, when he saw the three prisoners carrying iron hoops, and when they saw him they ran away. He managed to secure Kilroy, and subsequently appiThenaed the others. —The prisoners elected to be summarily dealt with, and they were each ordered to receive 12 strokes with the birch rod—John Coleman, a little boy, whs charged with steal- ing a quantity of scrap-iron, the property of the Widnes Foundry Company.—The case opus up on Monday, when Mr. C. Robinson gave evidence in behalf of the firm. He said he met the prisoner on Saturday in the Foundry yard, carrying a bag. He asked him what it contained, and he saidrags. He, however, was not satisfied with this explana- tion, and searched the bag. At the top were a few loose rags, and at the bottom a, quantity of scrap-iron. In reply to Inspector Barnett, witness said he valued the iron at about 2di—lnBpector Barnett said the prisoner had a sister who had been convicted of theft. His father was a chemical labourer.—Mr. Pilkington said it was a very sad case.— Inspector Barnett: The children seem quite lost.—Mr. Pilkington said a reformatory was the right place for a boy like the prisoner.—On the suggestion of the magistrates, Mr. Robinson withdrew the charge, owing to the prisoner being of such tender age. ANOTHEII JUVENILE ROBBERY.—Jpeeph Eccleston was convicted of stealing, on the 23rd inst., 12s. 6d., beionging to his master, John Jones, of Rainhill, and was ordered to receive 12 strokes with the birch rod.
LATEST NEWS.
_ - The coalmasters of Fife and Clackmannan on Thursday decided to refuse the men's demand for a rise of sixpence per day. •
The Right Hon. Lord Cranbrook will distribute the prizes to the successful students at the City of London College, on November 29th.

Mr. Healy, M. Y., arrived a Clonakilty on Thursday night, and a torchlight procession took place in hie honour. He afterwards addressed the people, advising them to adhere to the principles of the Land League. , • A Queenstown lady who wrote to the Premier urging the release of the suspects has received a reply from Mr. Glad- stone's secretary explaining that, in considering, the question of release, the Government must have regard solely to the condition of each district.

At a meeting of the proprietors of the East and West India Docks Company, held in London, yesterday, it was agreed, by an overwhelming majority, to carry out the directors' scheme, for forming new docks at Tilbury at a cost of £1,100,000.

The Rev. Walter Conway. of Clonbur, was sentenced to two months' imprisonment with hard labour, at Cong, yes- terday, for assaulting a bailiff, named James McGrath, who, at the suit of Lord Ardilaun, had .served him with a writ on board a vessel at Long Quay. A large meeting of County Waterford magistrates was held at Lismore yesterday, at which it was decided to pre- sent a memorial to the Lord Lieutenant praying that mili- tary force might be established at Lismore in consequence of an apprehended attack on the Duke of Devonshire's castle.

Captain Lloyd, the owner of the hone at New Pallas which was injured by an explosion of gunpowder on 11;mrs- day, attended the Petty Sessions, Limerick, yesterday, and made affidavits necessary to an application for compensation for injuries to his property. The gunpowder was placed out- side the window of the room where he usually slept, but, fortunately, on this occasion, he occupied another apart- ment.

j Late on Thursday night, a fatal accident occurred at the Bryncethin works, near Bridgend, where the Barrow Com- pany have been engaged some years in sinking operations. A shift of eight men were engaged in walling a shaft, when a fall of masonry took place, which carried the scaffold and men to the bottom of the pit. Four dead bodies were recovered from the debris. Three men are badly injured, and a fourth escaped miraculously with only a slight cut. THE FORTH BRIDGE Scantz.—The managers of the North British, Great Northern, North Eastern, and Midland Railway Co.'s travelled over the new route by which it is proposed to open communication between the north and south in connection with the Forth Bridge. It is proposed to establish a line from North Queensferry to Perth, by Dunfermline and Kinross, thereby greatly shortening the journey from Edinburgh northwards. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE COUNTY FRANCHISE.—Mr. W Banks, hon. eedfof the County oFranchise Association, has received the following, dated 10, Downing-street, September 28th :—"Sir,—Mr. Gladstone desires me to acknowledge the receipt of your letter, in which you ask, on behalf ef the County Franchise Association, and others, that he will receive a deputation for next session on the subject of the extension of the county franchise and the redistribution of seats. In reply, I am directed to say that he will not fail to bear in mind the request which you have preferred, but that he cannot at the resent moment undertake to give any pledge in the matter, as the time has not yet arrived for considering what measures her Majesty's Government should first choose far submission to Parliament.—l tan, sir, your obedient servant, E. W. HAMILTON." SERIOUS COLLIERY EXPLOSION AT WIGAN.

_ A serious explosion occurred early yesterday morning, at the Park-lane, Colliery, ne tr Wigan, belonging to the Garwood Coal and Iron Company. There were eleven men in the pit at the time, two of them in the nine fleet, and the others in the four feet seam. Help was quickly obtained and it was found that the nine feet seam had fired, and that the two men who were working there had been killed, but their bodies could not be recovered. The nine men in the other seam were got out in safety. _ ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

Tmobrro, Sept. 29.—A serious accident occurr7ed to-day near a;place called Aylmer to an excursion train which was on its way to the Exhibition grbunds at London. Five out of nine carriages composing the train were utterly wrecked. Six people were killed on the spot, and others, who are missing, are believed to be beneath the debris. Toacirrro, Sept. 29, Evening.—The railway collision which occurred to-day near Aylmer is ascertained to have been due to negligence on the part of the engine driver and fireman of the excursion, both of whom were killed. CLOSE OF THE COTTON "CORNER."

The Liverpool cotton "corner " closed at noon yesterday. There was a large crowd of brokers on the Liverpool Ex- change flags, but little excitement, it being understood that the greater part of the cotton sold to the cornerers had been either delivered or compounded for. At the last moment sales were effected at 7fd. to 7 7-1111., which are about the rates cnrrent during the past few days.

Another correspondent telegraphs :—Neon was the limit of time for meeting the engagements in what is known as the cotton " corner ' in Liverpool, and considerable interest was exelted as to the extent to -which the engagements would be met. Unusual activity prevailed on 'Change, the flags being thronged all the morning by an excited gather- ing of brokers and others. Upwards of 20,000 bales are said to have changed hands, but without any great fluctua- tion in price, the bulk being secured on behalf of one firm. I One transaction made at the last moment is said to have been cancelled in consequence of not being registered in time. It is said that all engagements were met, but there is a likelihood there will be a question raised as to the quilitv of some of the lots. The excitement was not so great as on the occasion of the last "corner."

THE QUEEN'S SYMPATHY WITH MRS. GARFIELD. The United States Minister, in London, has forwarded to the Queen a copy of the following telezram which has been received from the Secretary of State, at Washington, in reply to the enquiries of the Queen Its to the health of the the late President's 'wife and mother, and the request to be furnished with a good photograph of General Garfield. a Your telegram conveying the compassion of the Queen for the mother of the late President, was duly forwarded to Mrs. Garfield, at Menton, Ohio. I have just received the following reply: —'Please request Mr. Lowell to express to Her Majesty the Queen the grateful acknowledgements of the mother of General Garfield, and my own for the tender womanly Sympathy she has been pleased to send and also that Her Majesty's wish will be complied with at an early day.— LUCRE R. GARFIELD, You will please make fitting com- munication of this reply to Her Majesty."

ST. ANNE'S CRIIRCH.—FINANCIAL DIFFICIJLTII..9.—Ii was rumoured that St. Anne's Church, Warrington;was in dark- ness on Sunday evening last in consequence of the gas sup- ply having been cat off. On enquiry, however, the rumour turned out to be incorrect, but it transpired that such had almost been the case. For a long time the church finances have been in anything but a satisfactory condition, and as the gas bill bad not been paid for a considerable time, the vicar and churchwardens were notified that unless the bill was discharged before akertain day the supply of gas would be cat off. On the day named the money was not forth- coming. and the pipes were disconnected. One or two ardent friends interceded with the gas works officials on behalf of the church, and the pipes were connected for the evening service. A meeting of the congregation to discuss the finan- cial position of the church was held on Thursday morning, but was adjourned until next week. • WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY DETIkTING SOCIETY This society held its annual meeting on Monday last in Mr. Winskill's room, Bewsey-street, under the presidency of Dr. Huson• Mere. A Conservative whip had been issued, and it was announced by the Liberals that a question affecting the best interests of the society was to be con- sidered. The consequence was there was a large attend- ance. Or. Huson-More was proposed for re-election as Speaker.—His admirable conduct in the chair during last session was universally acknowledged, and the motion was carried unanimously. Much pleasure was expressed at the fact that though he was about to leave the town he would still be able to attend the meetings.—The Speaker said be did not apprehend that he should be absent from more than two or three meetings, and he was quite sure that if he were not present order would be maintained. Dr. Bowes was unanimously chosen as chairman of com- mittees. He said he hoped he should be able to render good service to the society. On the motion of the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, seconded by Mr. Henry Roberts, Mr. Finney was elected treasurer Land Mr. Isaac Leeson was appointed Clerk of the Howie on the proposal of Mr. Chapman. Mr. W. H. Harrison was ap- pointed his deputy. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and Mr. Thomas Flood were elected trustees of the property of the house. The following is the constitution of the Council:—Messrs. W. J. Burgess, Henry Roberts, Chap- man, George Woods, W. Dickens, C. J. Holmes, William Howard, with the officers of the house. The Speaker selected Mr. Smith as Sergeant-at-Arms. The most import- ant question was then considered :—Where should the meet- ings be held? The Rev. Richard Pilcher, 8.A., moved, and Mr. William Roberts seconded, that the Co-operative Hail should be engaged. As an amendment, Mr. Burgess moved that application be made for permission to hold the meetings at the Lecture Room of the Museum. This was seconded by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. A long discussion ensued in which was pointed out the general unsuitableness oef the Lecture Room, and eventually it was decidedto e.ngag the Co-operative Hall. The meeting then terminated

MONARCHY INRELATION TO THE PEOPLE. Sir,-1 have read with interest the letters of both your correspondents on the subject of "Monarchy in relation to the people," and wish to make a reinark or two on the same. I often think if the British taxpayer would ask himself a few questions as to what becomes of the money (between £600,000 and £700,000) annually spent to maintain royalty he would condemn the system that makes him pay that amount as one of the greatest ,absurdities. Let us take Her Majesty's income, which is £385,000 per annum. A lot of pleasure that to a poor working man, knowing that one individual is receiving such a sum out of our hard got earnings. We call poor people in the workhouses, who are unable to maintain themselves, paupers, because the parish supports them. We call Her Majesty the Sovereign, the State supports her. Now where is the difference? The State supports the one just the same as the parish supports the other; the only difference I can see is that what keeps I one in State would keep nearly 15,000 of the others in pan - perism, allowing each 10s. per wear. That is one item, for Mr. Bennett's consideration. Let us now take another. Thanks to somebody for giving us the Education Act ; if our fathers were no scholars, and we are not, perhaps our children may be, and will not sit down so tamely with the spending of the public money in maintaining luxurious Royalty. It day interest a few of your readers to give an item or two out of my Lord Chamberlain's department. The amount put down in the " Household Salaries" for that department is £66,499, which is a portion of the £385,000 paid annually by the State. Let us see what some of it is spent on. Upholsterers and cabinet makers, £11,381; joiners and blind makers, £1,038; locksmiths ironmongers, and armourers, £4,119 ; clockmakers, opticians, paper- hangers, and japanners, £2,447; total, £18,985. Now, sir, I think Her Majesty ought to have patent locks, first-class armour, and good ironmongery to cost the nation over £4,000 annually; but I never heard of Her Majesty wearing armour, though the nation has to pay for it. So much for my Lord Chamberlain's department. Well, there is for joiners, paperhangers, cabinet makers, &c., over £14,000 a year, although in 1379 it cost the Public Works Department over £43,000 to put the palaces in repair. Again, Mr. Bennett says that Royalty is constantly occupied in some good work or deed; but who pays for it? One item in the £385,000 per annum is for royal bounty, special services, alms and charity, £13,200. Against this we do occasionally see that Her Majesty has been most graciously pleases! to grant the sum of £lOO for the relief of sufferers by such-and-such a calamity. What a sham. It is easy to give other people's money, very easy to be occupied in some good work or deed at the expense of the public ; but can Mr. Bennett tell us of a single year in which the sum of £13,200 has been given by Her Majesty in charity, &c.? Yet the nation pays that sum every year, and as it is paid we have a right to know what becomes of it. Perhaps Mr. Bennett can tell us. In answer to his remarks about senti- ments and chivalry, I'm afraid if it was stript of the cash paid by the nation there would be but a small fraction of chivalric souls left to draw the 10,000 swords, or to die in defence of such a system. We want something more of fact, and less of fallacy ; we have had enough of that kind of government I have only given an item or two out of Her Majesty's income ; more could be given if time and space permitted. Hoping you will find room in your paper for the above remarks, I remain, Mr. Editor, yours, &c., Frodsham, Sep. 29th, 1881. A READER.

LIMN. BRITISH AND FOREIGN PIBLE SOCIETY.— MEETING AT LYMM. Under the presidency of Mr. J. Barton, J.P., the annua, meeting of the Lymm brahch of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in the Parochial Schools on Monday. There was a good attendance, and on the platform were the Revs. J. E. Symons (district secretary), J. Cullen, and S. Stafford. The CHA.IRMAN paid a tribute to the memory of the late district secretary, the Rev. Mr. Page. The object of the society was simply to distribute the Holy Scriptures with- out word or comment, to the various nations of the world, as far as possible; and over 200 translations of the Bible had been made in various languages. By this means they hoped to gain the confidence of all religions and denomina- tions. He had always had the utmost reliance and belief that the Bible issued by the society was God's word as He left it to us.—The Rev. t STAFFORD moved, "That this meeting desires to trecord its gratitude to Almighty God for the blessings He has vouchsafed to the efforts of this society , in the circulation of His word at home and abroad; and ' pledges itself to increased exertions toward the attainment of this object." When they heard of the success of the society, and how it had been the means of bringing men under the divine influence of the word, they would, he said, be prepared to support that resolution, and willing to make greater exertions in behalf of the society. (Applause.)—The Rev. J. E. SYMONS (deputation from the parent society) said he should be grieved indeed if in that meeting which had for its basis the word of God, which was the basis of all true freedom and the best source of consola- tion in suffering, be did not say one word about James Garfield, whose remains were being carried to the grave that day. Two nations had been united by a bond of earnest sympathy called forth by suffering ; and they would agree with him that it was fit that he should allude to the fact, when they were told that on the previous day a gentleman who had travelled in America told him that the late Presi- dent was a Bible-loving Christian, and that his whole life had been devoted, as _ far as in his power . .

lay, to circulating the word of God, bringing up his family in the truth which we learned from the word of God. NV hen be was taken away they would remember that charming message of tender sympathy that our Queen telegraphed to Mrs. Garfield, where she said words failed to express how deeply she felt for her in her sorrow and concluded "May God comfort and support you as He alone can." We were living in _days when the Bible was made much of, and also whet, some people said it had no power. He wondered if a man like Mr. Bradlaugh were to telegraph a message to Mrs. Garfield, to whom could he commend the widow, in the extreme hour of her bitter anguish, for sympathy and comfort and support. Not only our institutions but the throne and all connected with it were based in their truest outcome on the word of God. The question was often asked him as a representative of the Bible Society," What are you going to do with the revised version ?"- The position at present was this, that they did not know absolutely what 1, they were going to do. As the society was constituted they I were unable to circulate it. The first clause of the Bible Society's charter, which had stood for 77 year's, said that only the authorised revision could be circulated through England and Wales. The revised version was not the authorised one and whilst that clause existed it could not be circulated. It was intended shortly to call a meeting of the society's supporters in London, and put the difficulty before them, and if desirable, to ask permission from them so far to amend the first clause as to allow them to circulate side by side with the autborised version, the revised version. He believed the income of the society was about £4.000 below the previous year, but the sales had fallen off in England , by anticipation. Everybody had been looking forward for i the new version, and, they could readily understand how it had affected their sales. This year their sales had been still more affected, but it did not indicate a decreasing interest ' in the work of the society. The circulation in one month from the Bible house in London had decreased by 10,000 copies, but on the ether hand they had certain channels ' from which they derived an income. The free contributionshad increased by £4,000; therefore they were really doing well. Since the formation of the society 91 million copies had been issued in various languages, and during the past year three millions. Sunday schools were supplied at reduced prices, and the claims of workhouses, hospitals, gaols, the bedrooms of the hotels and waiting rooms at the railway stations were not neglected. A few days ago he passed through the London and North-Western station at Wigan, and finding there were no copies of the Scriptnres, he applied to the society, who in ide him a small grant. He sent half-a- dozen copies to Wigan and Crewe, and he expected to shortly do the same to Warrington. He referred to the work going on in Paris, making special mention of Dr. McCaw, Belgium, Spain, Roumania, and China. It had been a most difficult matter to get the Bible in Spain ; the priests were against them; but the Liberals had come into power, and the Minister of Public Worship had on more than one occasion declared himself in favoar of liberty of worship. They had every reason to believe that this liberty would be extended to the operations of the British and Foreign Bible Society. The sun of religious freedom had begun to dawn above the Spanish horizon. The society translated the Scriptures into 245 languages and dialects. Every language into which the word of God was translated and circulated was a new channel dug by human means in which the river of the water of life had to flow, and wherever it flowed fructified, and turned the desert into an oasis. Speaking of the mis- sionary societies, he said he did not know how the Bible Society would be able to carry on their work in connection with the great mission field were it not for the cordial help extended to them by all Evangelical Christian denomina- tions. (Applause.) He concluded by seconding the reso- lution moved by Mr. Stafford, which was carried.—Other speeches followed, and at the close a collection was made on behalf of the society.

Mr. W. H. Smith, M.P., in distributing the prizes at the Devon County School, west Buckland, on Wednesday, urged that education should be varied to meet the peculiar circumstances, wants, and habits of the people for whom it was intended, for if they insisted on imposing one cast-iron system, whether it was issued from Whitehall or elsewhere, the result would be of a most unsatisfactory character.

div.head: riOLIDAY EXCURSIONS.- -.WHERE TO GO AND WHAT 7io SEE.
div.p: riOLIDAY EXCURSIONS.- -.WHERE TO GO AND WHAT 7io SEE.

_ [Specrea. Most of us who are absorbed all the year round with the labours and anxieties apperta erang to our daily avocations look forward to taking a b'elei rest in the course of the sum- mer season and rush off to some distant spot where we can enjoy change of scem jeei for a time and then return to go through another Y' ext'A toil with renewed vigour and more cheerful spirits. Notwithstanding the fact that the weather has not been by any means favourable for holiday trips duunarienrtandn gssoie. portion of the latter part of this summer we that the number of persons who have availed thernselv,,es of the opportunities afforded them of going by the n'emerous "cheap trips" from this district to various attrective places has been very great. By far the greater member of people run down to the seaside or out into the country to spend their holidays. We, however, this year \having only a very short time at our disposal, resolved upon taking a trip to London, and as we selected a route which took us through some of the most picturesque and romantic scenery in England it has been thought that a brief account of what we saw upon our journey might not prove uninteresting. Taking our tickets by the Midland Railway, we left Warrington Central Station at 9-25 am. and were rapidly transported to Manchester from whence we pro- ceeded via Romiley Junction to Maple. After leaving Manchester the scenery became more and more interesting as we proceeded until after passing Marple we saw plaie indicatione of our being conveyed through the beautiful county of Derbyshire. Passing New Mills and Chapel-en- le-Frith we went on through tunnels, over viaducts, looking down upon some very old roads and up to still older hills, and around upon quarries, mills, factories, burial grounds, reservoirs, valleys, and rivulets, to the Peak Forest. In ancient times it is said that the forest was much infested by wolves, and we thought it somewhat singular that as we ap- proached the Peak Forest Station not a tree or shrub was to be seen, but the green fields were divided by stone walls only. One of our fellow travellers informed us that there is in the hamlet of Peak Forest an old chapel that was for- merly celebrated for " runaway marriages," and there- fore regarded as a kind of Derbyshire Gretea Green. Approaching Miller's Dale and Moneel Dale the scenery that met our gaze was really magnificent, more especially just previous to entering the tunnel after ' leaving Monsal Dale, for there the view of the river, in 1, pretty valley, with a large fish pan and waterfall, contri- buted to make up a splendid picture. We were now for a considerable distance whirled along beautiful scenery, ob- taining, as we passed Bakewell, a tine view of the noble old church and town, and having gone through a tunnel near Haddon Hall, the seat of the Duke of Rutland, we emerged to find ourselves gazing upon a magnificent panorama of lovely green slopes, dotted with trees, whilst in the valley before us was the river running in quite a zigzag direction for a long distance by the side of the line. Shortly after- wards we left Matlock Bridge, and subsequently obtained as we passed Matlock Bath, beautifully situated in Matlock Dale, a magnificent view of scenery which almost made us imagine for a moment that we had been suddenly trans- ported into Switzerland. Here almost every house appeared perched upon a hillock " seeking shelter from the higher Tors." Leaving Matlock Bath we obtained an uninterrupted view of the hill country and the Low Peak district, the Black Rocks, Lea Wood and Valley, and then drawing near to Cromford we were shown Willersley Castle, the seat of a descendant of Sir Richard Arkwright, the inventor of the "spinning jenny," and the cotton mill. Arkwright, who was "first a barber and afterwards an itinerant dealer in hair," was a Lancashire man, heviog been born at Preston, and is de,cribed by Thomas Carlyle as amid "stropping of razers, shaving dirty beards, and the contradictions and con- fusions attendant thereon—wheels and contrivances plying ideal within the same rather hopeless looking, which, how- ever, he did at last bring to bear." Cromford is also cele- brated as being, near the residence of Florence Nightingale, whose army of nurses did so much for our wounded and sick soldiers during the Crimean war. We next approached Ambergate Junction, and as we gazed upon the pretty wide valley spread out before us, we could not held thinking that we had passed through a number of the most beautiful scenes of hill and dale, rock and river, peak and forest, cloud and sunshine, as can be witnessed in any 'part of the United Kingdom. Passing Helper, with its picturesque cemetery, of which we had a good view, we soon afterwards saw Bunkers Hill surmounted by a solitary group of large trees, the Derby race course, and arrived at Derby, the centre of the Midland Railway system. Here total abstainers or others desirous of quenching their thirst without resort- ing to alcoholic drinks, have a chance of doing so without , leaving their seats, for a number of page boys attend each train with a goodly supply of f-esh milk, which, judging I from the quickness with which it is sold, is heartily appre- ciated on a warm summer's day. Leaving Derby we pro- ceeded along the beautiful and fertile valley of the Trent, catching glimpses of Trent College, Thumpton Hall (the seat of Lady Byron), to Loughborough, the most con- spicuous object in the town, seen from the line, being the I fine tower of the church of All Saints. Soon after this we came in sight of the range of Charnwood Hills, of which we have several picturesque views, and where, it is alleged, every description of stone in the world can be found, except three; and those geologists do not despair of finding there. Is we'were conveyed along by the river Soar, a tributary of the Trent, we noticed that this was a district much fre- quented by the disciples of old Isaac Walton, who were to be seen ever and anon busily engaged on the banks of the river. This reminded us of a tale we once beard of one of the old-fashioned clergymen of the Church of England, who was such a lover of piscatorial pursuits that his mind was engaged with them when it ought to have been occupied with matters of a inure sacred character. It is said that " one beautiful morning he was deeply engaged in angling in the silvery stream, when he was approached by an individual who was soon recognised as his parish clerk and who thus addressed him—' Please, sir, the place is full and the people are waiting for you." What place is full, and what people are waiting to see rne." Please, air, the church and the corgregation. It's Sunday you know sir." Bless my life I had forgotten it was Sunday. I'll be there in a minute or two." Doubtless most of our readers will say that if the story be true it is to be hoped that that class of clergy are now defunct. As we drew near to Leicester we had quite a panoramic view of the town with its fine spires and towers. Remaining here a few minutes we rapidly passed Wigston and Glen with their ancient churches, and arrived at Market Harboro', a favourite resort of hunting gentry. Passing through well cultivated agricultural districts in Northamptonshire and Bedfordehire, we noticed that between Derby and London every plot of land is evidently regarded as valuable by the farmer or gardener who holds it, and it was also patent that many of the agricultural operations there are now performed by machinery, thereby reducing the amount of labour. From Bedford to London the ride was very pleasant, excellent views of the country being obtained on both sides of the line, although, of course, nothing like so picturesque as the views which we had enjoyed through Derbyshire. Leaving Bedford we came to Luton and soon after had a glimpse of Dallow Farm, in 3 loft of which it is said old John Bunyan hid from his pursuers. This was one of the places "where in the reign of Charles H. Dissenters held their unlawful conventicles." The next place of interest that we noticed as we pessed was the old city of St. Albans, in the centre of which stands "the clock tower where is preserved the curfew bell that in days of Norman rule tolled the knell of parting day." Soon after this obtaining distant views of Harrow, Willesden, St. John's Wood, &mew° found ourselves approaching the great city, and stopping a few minutes at Kentish Town to collect tickets, we shortly afterwards arrrived at St. Pancras, which with its magnificent hotel is supposed to constitute the grandest terminus in the world. From here we betook ourselves by the 'Metropolitan railway to Kensington, and having secured a , I place at our hotel we strolled into Kensington Gardens, which are 200 acres in extent, are very pretty, but are, in fact, more of the nature of a park than gardens, and are in reality an extension of Hyde Park. Kensington Palace, the place where our Queen was born, is situated just inside the gardens. Passing by the Round Pond and the back of the Albert Memorial we entered Hyde Park, and going round by Rotten Row were rewarded with a sight of the fashionable world. Our companion informed us that every evening during the season the Princess of Wales with her two daughters are to be seen in the Row for about an hour, and the obeisance made to her shows that she is exceedingly popular with all classes of society. Just at this time of the evening too the Row is crowded, and the sight of the elite of London on horseback, or in their carriages, is one not soon forgotten. London offers such a vast num- ber of attractions to visitors that we will not attempt to weary our readers with anything like a description of them, but content ourselves with merely referring to some of the principal places of interest we visited. The next day after our arrival being Sunday, we strolled into St. Paul's Cathedral, and, remaining to the service, we had the pleasure of listening to the massive chords of rich harmony poured forth by the powerful organ, which were heard to advantage under the great dome. We subsequently visited Westminster Abbey, within the venerable walls of which repose the ashes of kings, queens, and a hest of notable men whose names are revered throughout the civilised world. The following afternoon ,we paid a visit to the magnificent pile of buildings known as the Houses of Parliament, wherein the sittings of the great council of England are held. Here we met with our esteemed borough member,Mr. J. G. McMinnies, by whose kindness and courtesy we were enabled to go through the principal portions of the building. The extent of the structure may be imagined when it is remembered that it comprises nearly 500 apartments, including the Houses of Lords and Commons. Entering by way of the members' entrance from Westminster Hall we were conducted into , the lobby where members find petitions which have been sent to them for presentation, from which we descended to the crypt of St. Stephens—the most superbly decorated crypt that we ever saw, being a per I ect little gem. Returning, we entered the room where Cromwell signed the warrant for the execution of Charles 1., and from thence to the House of Commons. This evening an important debate was about to take place, and looking around we saw more than half the seats already occupied by hats,aithough it yet wanted nearly two hours to the time when the Speaker would take the chair. Passing through several lobbies we visited the libraries where we saw several of the more prominent ohthell Lords, terrace adjoining, members of th e Lower House, includingeour old tovensmari. Mr. Peter Rylands, all of whom appeared to be buisily en- gaged whilst waiting for the debate to commence. We next entered the luxurious chember known as the House an edwtrhe w e after numerous merous lobbies, vestibules, and enjoyed a which we strolldescendedin th to fa e cobl evening en the river side, with an interesting view

RECOGNITION MEETING AT WARRINGTON. To welcome the Rev. J. Eglinton and the Rev. Thomas Rippon, the newly-appointed ministers of the Warrington circuit of Wesleyan Methodists, a meeting was held in Bewsey-road Chapel, on Monday evening. There was a very good attendance. Mr. Robert Cook presided, and there were also present :—The Rev. J. Eglinton, Rev. J. Agar Beet, Rev. T. Rippon; Messrs. A. Lamplugh, M. Bowden, E. B. Bowser, J. Suminersgill, J. Brown (Lymm), J. Hen- shall, J. Shaw Green, ,kc. The CHAIRMAN, after expressing his pleasure at being present, referred to the death of Mrs. Coleman, and said they knew Mr. Coleman was removed from Warrington on account of Mrs. Coleman's health. It was hoped by a re- moval to a more congenial and salubrious climate Mrs. Col- eman might be restored, or ,it any rate that her life might be prolonged, but God in His Providence had seen fit to call her to himself. At the meeting that day resolutions had been carried that expressions of their deep sympathy and th,:ir earnest regard for Mr. Coleman in his affliction should be sent to him. He went on to remark that it was fortunate for them as a community that they belonged to an ecclesiastical system that in any case where they lost a minister another was forthcoming. They deplored Mr. Coleman's loss, but Providence had sent a man who, he thought, would in every respect be heartily received by them. He trusted what Mr. Coleman had sown and watered would presently be reaped in abundance, and that of the seed which had been sown the harvest would soon be I gathered in and the society greatly increased. The Rev. Mr. Eglinton was appointed to be their superintendent. He was a man who stood well in the ranks of Methodism, who had occupied some of the best circuits, and had filled many of the various offices of the church. He came to them full of the Holy Ghost and fire, and he believed Mr. Eglinton was sent to be of immense use, to them. He trusted success would attend his every step. (Hear, hear.) They also knew that Mr. Hagen, whom they loved, and whom they had listened to with the greatest delight, profit, ' and edification, had been lain aside. It would have been cruel in them if they had insisted upon his staying in the circuit as one of their ministers, because he felt the small labour Mr. Hagen would be able to give to the congregation I would be quite as much as could be expected from him, at any rate, for a time. Mr. Hagen also had been removed.] from them, and in his place they had a man full of life, I health, and vigour. He had not had the pleasure of hearing Mr. Rippon preach, but he had heard a capital account of him. He had no doubt he would edify everyone of them, and would fulfil their expectation. He (the chairman) , was looking back with his brother the previous night, and he found he had been in Warrington more than quarter of a century, and they had bad 24 ministera in the circuit dur- ing that time. They had had seine first-rte men. That chapel had been built through the energies, activities, and spiritual mindedness of some of those men; and they had I grown to what they were partially because of them. They I were looking for some better, higher, and more glorious days than those they had passed, and he prayed that it might be continued to them to increase from week to week and year ' to year until they became far greater than they were at present. (Applause.) The Rev. J. EGLINTON, who was greeted with applause, then addressed the meeting, and gave an account of his conversioe. He expressed his sympathy with Mr. Coleman and Mr. Hagen, and said he would try in all circumstances, i and at all times, to do the best he could. He would promise as little as he could, but would do as much as he could. He would always do the best he could in the pulpit, as he held that was the first work of a Methodist preacher. The second work was pastoral visitation. The persons he would look to would be the halt, the sick, and the poor—(applause)—and in reference to the well-to-do people he would be as respect- ful as he could, and he had no doubt they would help him on quite as much as he would find it good for him. (Ap• plause.) Mr. A. LA1[21.13011, after remarking that circumstances over which they had no control had changed their ministers, and that Mr. Coleman's name would be a household word in the circuit for many years, referred to the state of the society. He said they were never in a higher state of financial and spiritual prosperity than they were that day. (Hear, hear.) They had more spacious places of worship, and they had a most noble staff of local preachers. (Ap- plause.) He contrasted that the barn-like structures of former days to the present commodious places of worship, and stated that the value of the property of the circuit had increased from £9,000 to £30,000. Referring to the ministers, he observed that they never had a more noble staff of ministers than they had to- day. (Applause.) He had no doubt if Mr. Hagen had health and strength he would rank amongst the greatest preachers of Methodism. (Applause.) As to the Rev. Joseph Agar Beet, his name was known in all churches. (Applause.) He was sure they all wished the new ministers happy in their homes, happy in their hearts, and happy in their social relationships with the people ; and that the smile of God might rest upon their efforts in that church. (Applause.) The Rev. J. A. BEET spoke upon getting good, and stated that the two chief defects of the Methodist people generally were the lack of regular growth in Christian life after con- version, and the,intellectual study of the Bible. The Rev. Thomas Ripon and others also addressed the meeting.

Cnonctt MisstosAux SOCIETY.—The annual sermons on behalf of this society were preached on Sunday, at Wharton church, by the Rev. R. Palmer, late of China, and the Rev. C. Cay, LL B.; the vicar. Also at the Weaver schools (the church being pulled down) by the incumbent in the morn- ing and the missionary from China in the evening. There was a children's service in the afternoon in Wharton church, to which parents and the different school children were invited. The joint missionary Meeting was held in the Wharton schools on Tuesday evening, when the Revs. Palmer, Youard, Nixon, and Cory, took part. The collec- tions after each service raised a nice sum for the parent society after the few local expenses were defrayed. WESLEYAN NEW CHAPEL—Services on behalf of the new chapel, which the Wesleyans of Winsford purpose erecting soon, were held on Sunday and Thursday. On the former day two sermons were preached by the Rev. F. Haines, of Northwich. In the e7ening the congregation was good, but only fairish in the morning, though the sermons were worthy of a chapel full both times. The United Methodist Free Church was lent them for Thursday, when sermons were preached by the Rev. James Ritchie, of Sandbach, in the afternoon, and the Rev. Richard Roberts, of Liverpool, in the evening, with a tea meeting in the interim of the two services. The collections and proceeds of the tea were devoted to the new chapel scheme. OVER PRIMITIVE METHODISTS.—At the High-street Primitive Methodist Chapel two sermons were preached on Sunday last by the Rev. J. Shepherd, of Bradley Green. The choir sang two anthems with considerable spirit, and the collections were good. SCIENCE CLASSES, WINSFORD.—The enrolment of students for the winter sessions in science and art will take place next week preparatory to the re-opening of the Academy Government classes in physiography, acoustics, light,.heat, magnetism and electricity, and chemistry, Sze. The princi- pelt:l\lr. Buckley, will have the advantage of studying the three next sessions under Professor Roscoe, of Victoria University, the Gcverninent Science Department haying undertaken to pay three-fourths of his University fees till June next, for Friday afternoon's and Saturday's classes.

NEIVTON POLICE Cockr.—At this court, on Saturday, 1 Colonel McCorquodale presiding, John Clut was chated with having been found in pursuit of game near Burton- wood, on the 10th June. It was stated thar the prisoner I was seen crossing a corn field in the occupation of Mr. Gleave along with three others, who had several dogs with them. They appeared to have found game and were follow- ing it up. They all ran away on seeing the police, but as prisoner was known he was afterwards apprehended. The Bench fined the prisoner 40s. and costs, or one month's tin- prisonment.—Two young men named William Massey and Thomas Allen were each fined 2s, Gd. and costs for riding a bicycle on the footpath. It was stated by Allen that the constable did not ask him to stop, but put his stick into the wheel, and caused him to fall against the wall. The wheel of the bicycle was broken, and bad cost him 3s. 6d. for repait s. PnovisroNA.l, LicnxcE.—At the Newton ad jot rned licensing sessions, on Saturday, Mr. ktowbottorn, of Wigan, appeared to make application in reference to a provisional licence to a house about to be built at Glazebrook Junction. An application was made in the first instance so far back as 1875, but up to the present time the house had not been built. The person who made application then had since abandoned his plans, and did not intend to go on with them. The provisional grant was applied,for in 1879 by his client and granted. The house had not yet been quilt because the ' line had not been opened, and so there was no immediate need for house but lie wished the magistrates to say whether the provisional licence was still in existence.—The bench ' said they coasidered the provisional licence still in existence.
