before us of Lambeth Palace, and a host of other places of interest. At five o'clock we were introduced to the House of Lords, where the Lord Chancellor had just taken his seat on the Woolsack. We remained here during the whole of the time that their lordships sat attending to their arduous k, duties of reviewing the work of the House of Commons—a period of twenty minutes! We came away more firmly im- pressed than ever with the belief that the Upper Chamber, as at present constituted, is worse than useless, and that it is high time that it should be recon- stituted. Having visited the Horse Guards, the Westminster Aquarium, St. James's Park, and the Green Park, we re- turned to our hotel, and afterwards caught an express train , from St. Pancras station, which conveyed us back to War- rington through the same beautiful and romantic scenery' as we had witnessed on our journey up. We need scmcely add that having crowded so much sight-seeing into our 1 brief holiday wd returned home well pleased with having ' taken the route we did. RAMBLER.

pelted to all parts of the system, and as thislpropulsion took place along elastic tubes, it was evident that physiology must include a knowledge of the simple laws of the move- ments of fluid along such tubes. The physiologist must be mechanician enough to comprehend the questions of in- ternal pressure in tubes with elastic walls ; the question of the action of a propelling pump; the question of the opera- tion of valves. He must further understand mechanics enough to comprehend clearly the action of levers, since the bones which the muscles moved were simply a series of levers obeying mechanical laws. He must be physicist enough to understand the regulation and distrioution of the I heat of the body—a purely physical question. He must know something of the laws of sound, or he would wholly fail to comprehend the function of hearing. He must be optician enough to enable him to understand the projection of images upon the sensitive parts of the eyeball. The operation of digestion was perhaps as important as any in the body of our personal wellbeing, and yet for the most part it was not specially of vital account. It could be performed as well outside the body as inside—doubtless many wish that it were. (Laughter.) Practically, the digestion of food, or its preparation for 'being absorbed into the general system, was a chemical operation which could be repeated very exactly in an oven. So that we must reckon chemistry as another necessary auxiliary of physiology. But, besides these chemical, physical, and mechanical processes, of which he had just given some simple examples, there were the special vital phenomena, which were the particular pro- perty of the physiologist. Such was the scope of phy- siology. What were its advantages P They had seen that physiology treated of the phenomena of life. They had further seen what different hypotle ass of life have from time to time dominated the science, nd it would be readily understood how the particular view it life which happened to be held had influenced its progress. Not only had phy- siology been modified by these hypotheses, but the science of medicine which is founded on it has curiously enough derived inspiration from the same views. Thus when life was considered as a separated entity, so also was disease, and remedies were (logical), enough) all constructed in accordance with the theory. The laws of physiology taught each one what to eat and drink, and what to avoid. It indicated the special kind of food best adapted for each person's particular refreshment, and whilst teaching us the use and value of different articles of food, it showed how and in what proportions they should be combined to form a suitable and nutritious diet. It taught them when to eat or drink and when to abstain, how to dress, why they. were warm, and how to keep so. In short, it taught them how to live and maintain health, so that the termination of life, which at its normal time was natural as life itself, should not be hastened. Finally it showed very clearly what to expect from a violation of its laws. Were the laws of physiology but more generally known they would hear much less of such anti-physiological doctrines as absolute vegetarianism. There would boa greater appreciation of the benefits of vaccination, and a deeper con- viction of the value of sanitary reform, and last, but not least, there would be less fashion in deformity. (Laughter and applause.) "No knowledge could be so incessantly I appealed to by the incidents of every day as the knowledge of the processes by which man lived and acted. At every ' moment he was in danger of disobeying laws which, when disobeyed, might bring years of suffering, decline of powers, and premature decay. Sanitary reformers preached in vain, because they preached to a public which did not understand the laws of life—laws as vigorous as those of gravitation or motion. Even the sad experience of others yielded no lessons, unless they understood the principles involved. If one man was seen to suffer from vitiated air, another was seen to endure it without apparent harm; a third concluded that it was all chance,' and trusted to that chance. Had he understood the principle involved, he would not have been left to chance and his first lesson in swimming would not have been a shipwreck." (Applause.) Councillor MONKS proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer for his very able and very interesting lecture. He said the study of physiology, he was quite sure, was one of those subjects which would well repay any young man or any lady who mould take to it. It occurred to him, when Dr. Young was speaking, that he might, if diposed, give a lecture, or a series of lectures, on what he would call a study of the laws of health. He was quite certain there were a great m iny people in Warrington who would be glad to listen to such lectures, that they wouldbe greatly benefited by them, and would assist the sanitary authorities of the town very much. He hoped such a course of lectures would be given. They need not interfere with the science class, but they could be given in a popular form—such as the one that had been given that night—and he was sure they would be well attended. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. FINNEY, in seconding the proposition, said he had enjoyed a great treat, and he was sure he was speaking the sentiments of those present when he said he believed they had done the same. (Applause.) He could only express a hope that the result of the lecture would be a large acces- sion of young men, and he might say old members, to the class. (Applause.) One of the chief characteristics of the lecture to his mind has been its simplicity. The language with which Dr. Young had clothed hie ideas and sentiments was such that ce uld not by any possibility have been mis- understood by even the youngest pr ‘sent. (Hear, boa'.) He expressed a hope that the lectures might be repeated, and said teose who took an interest in education were greatly indebted to the gentlemen who were at the head of the classes for the manner in which they were bringing for- ward such gentlemen as Dr. Young and others to lecture to them. (Applause.) The LECTURER briefly acknowledged the vote of thanks. On the proposition of Councillor BURGESS, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, and the proceedings terminated.

div.head: " PHYSIOLOGY : WHAT IS IT "
div.p: " PHYSIOLOGY : WHAT IS IT "

INTERESTING LECTURE BY MR. A. H. YOUNG. Ma. A. H. Young, F.R.C.S., delivered a lecture entitled 'Physiology: What is it ? " in the Lecture Room, at the Warrington Museum, on Tuesday evening, as the inaugural address in connection with the physiology class of the School of Science. There was a good attendance, andl amongst those present were Messrs. F. Monks, D. W. Finney,' J. H. Gornall, C. Chorley, T. Grime, J. Turner (Penketh),W:l D. Jeans, J. Taylor, J. Rhymer Young, C. Jackson Holmes (hon. sec.), dm. The chair was occupied by Dr. Starkey Smith. The CRAIRMAN, in introducing the lecturer, said he had no doubt, from the very well-known character and great ability of Mr. Young, that they would have a very interest- ing and very instructive lecture. He hoped that the result of the lecture that night would be that a great number of young men would enrol themselves for this class of physi- ology. He believed it was just a question whether this class of physiology would be conducted this session unless there were more students enrolled than last year. He did not lueow that he need detain them any longer by making any preliminary remarks, and therefore he had very great pleasure in calling upon Mr. Young to deliver his address. The LECTURER, who was applauded on rising, said when he was requested to open the class of physiology with a short address which should at the same time be explanatory of the science itself, and also indicative of the advantages afforded by it, he accepted the invitation with no little hesitation, because written addresses of an introductory nature were not his forte, and because not being a physiolo- gist, he had no special authority to speak upon the par- ticular subject of physiology. Whilst thus foreshadowing many deficiences in what, under the stress ef other work, had necessarily been a hurriedly prepared address, he never- theless ventured to hope that he might be so far successful in his efforts to point out the objects, and advantages of physiology that the regular course of lectures on this sub- ject, which were to be delivered during the session just in- augurated, might at least be sufficiently well attended to justify its continued existence. The subject conveniently divided itself into two parts—(l) What is physiology? (2) " What advantages does a knowledge of it bestow? Turn- ing their attention, in the first place, to the former of these questions, let them consider for a moment the term itself. Physiology irriplied the study of nature generally, and such, apparently, was its primary signification. Subsequently, however, the term had become more restricted in its application, and physiology might now be broadly defined as the science which treated of the phenomena of life. Thus it included a consideration of the uses or functions of all living structures, irrespective of which of the great kingdoms of nature they might belong to. Animal and vegetable physiology were therefore but sub- divisions of one science. But the importance of man's position in the chain of animal existence had raised him to the dignity of special study, and by human physiology was meant the knowledge of the uses or functions of the human body or of the various parts of which it was composed. Hence the common but somewhat unphilosophical division of physiology into vegetable, animal, and human. It must be understood that human physiology was but a special section of animal physiology, in that it was the physiology of a special class. So far as definitions went they had learn.- then, that physiology had the study of life as its sole object, and at once a very natural question forced itself to the front, viz., " What is life? " Probably there were few persons who had not asked themselves that question, and speculated as to the nature of that subtle something, by virtue of which they lived, moved, and had their being. Who had not wondered at that marvellous power which enabled them to think? Who had not wondered at the power which determined the evolution of a plant from the seed ? Who had not wondered at the de- velopment of a chick, with its bones, muscles, nerves, feathers, and other apparently widely different structures, from the yolk of a single egg, in itself comparatively struc- tureless ? What was life ? So far as he knew no. satisfac- tory answer had been given to the question. Still it was necessary they should know something about it, as he hoped to show that the science of physiology had from time to time been necessarily modided in conformity with diverse theories as to the nature of life. Physiology had always borne a direct relation to the truth of its fundamental laws. By the early physiologists life was regarded as an in- dependent principle, capable of being added to or removed from dead matter. They assumed the existence of two distinct things—dead material and a living prin- ciple. Life was an entity which occupied the body much as living beings inhabited dead houses. The fable of Prometheus, who, it was recorded, succeeded in animating a marble statue with fire stolen from heaven, was but an allegorical expression of that conception of life. Similarly it was illustrated by the efforts of the numerous talented but visionary thinkers who had so diligently sought for the elixir of life, which, when found, should enable them to bestow life or prolong it for ever. One might readily anticipate that total failure was the result of all these efforts, but, curiously enough, one success was tecorded, even so recently as the 12th or 13th century. If all history were to be believed, Albertus Magnus, with the help of his favourite pupil, Thomas Aquinas, constructed a brazen statue which he animated with his elixir of life. They were further in- formed that the statue was exceedingly useful as a domestic servant, that it not only could speak, but was actually very talkative, and, indeed, at times noisy. The latter fault ceased its, should he say death, for it proved so annoying on one occasion whilst Aquinas was busily engaged on a mathematical problem that he took up is hammer and destroyed the statue, very much, it was added, to the annoy- ance of hit master. Later on physiologists thought life, like matter, was supposed to possess a life of its own. The body of an animal or plant was but the aggregation of a multitude of particles associated together in a par- ticular evay, the association determining the manifestation of their functions. Death was but the dissolution of one of these associations ; the particles were simply set at liberty to wander about until they were once more combined with other associations of similar particles. Life was now re- garded simply as a condition of matter ; that was to say that certain bodies might possess properties of a special character which they balled vital, using the term precisely as they used physical in relation to other properties. These special vital or living properties were an inherent power of growth—irritability, or the property of responding to a stimulus by an evolution of energy; contractility assimila- tion, by which was meant the power of converting food stuffs into material like unto itself ; and, lastly, the power of reproduction. Of the true nature of any of these vital properties, as indeed also of the so-called physical pro- perties they wete ignorant. It was from their effects alone that they inferred their existence. Thus, if a boby after being extended or twisted returned to its original shape, they said it was elastic So if another presented the power of growth and assimila- tion, was irritable or contractile, they said it lived ; and just as it was a fact that only certain bodies evidenced the phenomena of elasticity, or that electricity was only made manifest by certain bodies which they called conductors, so also the phenomena. ef life required a special and definite form of matter for their manifestations. This Professor Huxley had well called the physical basis of life, for so far as they knew life was never manifest except through its agency; probably it would be more familiarity known to them under the name of protoplasm or bioplasm. Thus a microscopically minute speck of apparently structureless jelly, looking like the white of an egg, might evidence per- fectly the phenomena of life in their entirety. It was born, grew, maintained itself by taking food into its interior and exercising that marvellous selective power by which it re- tained only that which it needed and rejected the remainder. It was irritable and contractile. It repro- duced its like, and ultimately died. The cycle of its life's history was complete. Higher forms of life were but the aggregations of similar bodies which, more or less modified, constituted the structurat units of a complex organism, in which the principle of the division of labour relegating to certain structural units special portions of the total walk done by the whole had led to the formation of tissues and organs—in short, to organization, namely, the existence of a definite structure. Organization in this sense, at least, was the result and not the cause of life. The lecturer here described at length the phenomena of life, by tracing the life history of one of the lowest forms of life— illustrating his remarks by means of the blackboard—and pointed out more particularly the results of a physiological division of labour upon the societies of such bodies which made up a more complex organism. He then proceeded to say that for the purposes of a class on animal physiology it still remained to be explairted what physiology was. Like many another person, casting about for a clear mode of exposition, he found it easier to begin his explanation by showing what phy- siology was not. Well, it was not anatomy. Anatomy told them the composition of the body and of the different organs of the body. It showed them the structure of muscular fibre, and how it was fixed to the bone. It showed the machinery of respiration, circulation and digestion; but not the meaning or purpose of these arrangements. It was true that by clever guess they could often say, from the mere inspection of a structure or organ, what its probable action was. They might surmise. from the fact that muscles were fixed to rigid jointed bones, that muscles were contractile and intended to move those bones ; but such knowledge (if knowledge it cculd be called) was always uncertain, and many instances could be referred to of the most absurd hypotheses as to the use or function of an organ based upon the study. of its structure only. Thus the arteries, which everyone knew now-a-days were blood channels and contained fluid blood, were for long enough believed to be air tubes. simply because they were usually found empty after death. To attempt to de- termine function from structure merely, was just as if a per- son with no knowledge of the power of steam, should from the mere inspection of a resting engir.e attempt to explain the function or operation of its various parts. Anatomy dealt with the dead inactive organ, and knowledge of action based on such a study was pure inference and surmise which had never been certified by an appeal to nature. Physiolo y dealt with the action of living and moving parts; it ‘egle the knowledge of anatomy explained and inspired by appeal to nature in another of her modes. If they haadrifeosly- lowed his picture of the body of an animal as a society of units, which, however modified, were still working to- gether for one common purpose, they would already suspect that physiology was a very hybrid and all compre- hensive study. To begin with, though physiology was not anatomy, still no one could be a physiologist who did not know the anatomical structure of the body. That was suf- ficiently obvious. To understand the motion of a steam engine they must at least know that it had a cylinder a piston, a crank, and a connecting rod. As the fluid in as hich was suspended oxygen carrying units had to be pro.

div.head: .... . DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: .... . DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.

TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. Edward Greenall (Chairman, James' Maroon, and Robert Pierpoint. MISCELLANEOUS.—James Simpson, carter, was charged with not having proper control of the horse of which he was in charge, at Appleton, on the 6th inst. Defendant was ridiag in his cart without reins. Ordered to pay ss. 6d. costs.—John Smith, of Wilderspool, was charged with keep- ing a house for the sale of milk without having it registered. Fined ss. and Ps. 6d. costs. TRESPASSING ix PURSUIT OF GAME.—SOAIMeI Rustage, William Jefferson, and Joseph Rudd, were charged with having been in unlawful pursuit of game, and with having nets and sett pegs in their possession, which had been used for taking game. P.& Booth said about eleven o'clock on the night of the 31st August, he saw the prisoners corning down the road at Stockton Heath, and he searched them. Jefferson bad a net containing partridge feathers, tied round his body, and Rustage and Rudd, had each a net and peig in their possession. The nets were wet and contained grass, and appeared as if recently used.—James Bailey, gamekeeper for Sir Gilbert Greenall, said about nine o'clock the same evening he saw the prisoners come from a gate which opened into two plantations. He folio red them, and saw Jefferson throw a net over a hedge into a garden. He was present when prisoners were searched and the nets appeared to have been recently used.—Prtsoners were fined £5 including costs, or a month's imprisonment. On the application of the Inspect.or the Bench granted an order for the destruction of the nets. DISGRACEFUL ASSAULT twos A FATIIER.—Edward Wil- kinson was charged with having, on the 22nd ult., assaulted his father, John Wilkinson, who is 70 years old.—C.a.n- plainant said he was going home from Mr. Beswick's gm den, where he had been planting some trees, when he was over- taken by his son. They walked side by side for some distance, and the son upbraided him with going on the parish. When they got opposite defendant's sister's house defendant said "I have helped to bring up this and now they have thrown you upon the parish for us to keep." Complainant then hit him with a small stick, and defendant tht`ew him to the ground. He seized him by the throat with the left band, and with his right he struck him ea the face many times.—Sarah Rohinson, complainant's daughter, confirmed his statement. Defendant was partially drunk.—Mr. Moore, who defended, endeavoured to have the the case settled amicably, but complainant wished it •to go on. He characterised the case as a most painful one, and said the complainarit first struck the . defendant several times with a stick:and then seized his finger with his teeth. Defendant used no more force than he thought was necessary to release himself.—Frances Wil- kinson was called in support of this statement, and the defendant was fined 20s. and us. 6d. costs, or in default, a month's imprisonment. —Mr. Greenall said it was most disgraceful for defendant to assault his father in that way. CHARGE OF THEFT AGAINST A GIRL.—A girl named Mar- garet Ellison, alias Wimperley, was charged on remand with having, on the 27th August, stolen 7s. ld., the money of her master, Samuel Sutton, of Latchford.—Mr. Moore appeared for the defendant.—Mr. Nicholson, deputy magis- trates' clerk, said be had received a note from the prosecutor, in which he said he would be unable to appear that day, as , he had only just returned from the Isle of Man, where he had been on account of his health, and he was too unwell to undergo the anxiety. With the permission of the magistrates, he was perfectly willing to withdraw from the prosecution, as he had no wish to send the girl to prison. —Mr. Moore said, when the case was heard at the occa- sional courthouse, Mr. Sutton stated he knew nothing about the matter; it was his wife who was the chief witness.—The Bench adjourned the case until next sessions. THE JUNIOR OVERSEER FOR WHITLEY SUPERIOR CEN- SURED.—Mr. Mo.e.re, solicitor, applied for a license to sell beer to be consumed off the premises at a shop occupied by Wm. Worrall, at Whitley Superior. The case had been adjourned to allow Alfred Barber, overseer, to prove that the value of the premises was under £l2, which tie had stated to be the case.—Mr. Barker said he had tad the premises examined by Mr. Owen who, how- ever, could not attend.—He handed in a note in which Mr. Owen said the value of the premises was considerably more supportth than that Barber's cell t a sel:l—e y mwr. e.re‘eloaosrsee scs r.h je co . E.u\lvdrignioltt .elldl'edanMd who deposed that the nett annual value of the premises was Greenall, in granting the license, said he must ~:otest against the course which Barber had adopted. He ilad really treated the Bench as insane people. He had sworn at the last sessions that the house was only worth £ll, and now his own valuer said he could not support him. The magistrates thought he had not treated them with proper respect—Mr. Pierpoint agreed with the Chairman. It was perfectly unjustifiable foe anybody to go to that court, who knew perfectly well the course which ought to be taken, and took up its time with an objection which any sensible person knew was not correct—Mr. Moore applied for costs, but the Cleric &aid that the Bench had net power to grant the application.

div.head: RUNCORN' COUNTY COURT,
div.p: RUNCORN' COUNTY COURT,

'ruzsaky.—Bef ore Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. I CLAIM Fba BOARD AND LODGING.—Wm. Smith, Briscoe- street,Dukes-fied, mimed from Thomas Forshaw, fiatman, Bentinck-street, the sum of £1 14s. for board and lodging. —Plaintiff said defendant agreed to pay 13s. per week, and for some time he did so, but left a balance amounting to the sum stated.—The Judge gave a verdict for the plaintiff for £l6s.

A WOMAN TAMEN INTO CUSTODY FOB CONTEMPT OF Couar.—Mr. Nicholson, registrar, had a case before him in which George Hadcock, a Shopkeeper living at Weston, sued Mary Hagan,. of the same place, for £1 4s. 2d., being the value of goods supplied. The evidence showed that the debt was contracted by defendant's husband, who died two years ago. She was left with eight children, but she stated that except some furniture and £l6 from the club which she received, 'she had nothing with which to maintain the family. Under these circumstances, she said she could not pay the debt. She married again in March of the present year.—The Registrar said that unless if was Droved that some money had been left by the husband with which to pay his debts, he could not make an order. He would, how- ever, refer the matter to the judge.—The case was afterwards taken before His Honour, who made an order for the pay- ment of 3s. per month.—The defendant (excitedly) : I cannot pay it, I tell you.—The Judge: I think you can pay 38. a month.—The defendant (to plaintiff) : I will give you a black eye on the other side of your face.—The Judge: Is the officer of the court here? Give this woman into custody. —Mrs. Hagan was then given in charge.—At the termina- tion of th 4 business the prisoner was called into the witness box, and the Judge, addressing her, said: You made use of very, violent language when you came before me in my room.—The prisoner: I beg your pardon, sir.—His Honour (continuing) : Language that I cannot permit to be used in a court of justice. I have the power to send you to gaol, and I have a very great mind to do so. You ought to know better than to use language of that kind in a court of justice—to threaten a witness who appears against you because justice is given in a matter. I have otdered you to be detained here, and, I regret, for the sake of example, that the court does not it later, for I would have kept you till the last hour, and that would have been sufficient punishment. Allow me to tell you that if ever you behave in that manner before me agairt I shall send you to gaol. Take care how you behave when- ever you come into a court of justice again.—The woman then left the box. CLAIM AGAINST POTATOE DEALERS.—SamueI, Clarke, innkeeper, Overton, sued Mr. George Eastwood, potato dealer, Lowerhead-row, Huddersfield, for £9 68 sd, the price of potatoes supplied to him. Mr. Burton represented the. plaintiff, to whom a verdict WAS given for the full amount claimed.—Mr. Burton also appeared for Mr. Clarke in a second ease, in which he claimed £4 108 from Mr. Job Rutter, potatoe dealer, Brunswick-street, Runcorn. His Honour made an order for payment at the rate of 108 per month.

ACTION FOE MONEY LEarr.—Mr. Thomas Bate, of Aston, sued Mr. William Percival. Little Leigh, for the sum of £7 14s, alleged to have been lent to him previous to his liqui- dating.—Mr. Burton represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Jolliffe (from the office of Messrs. Ashton and Garrett) for defendant.—lt appeared that notice had been given on Fri- day last of the withdrawal of the case; ard it was, there- fore, not proceeded with. No costs were given for the time after the notice of withdrawal. FALLING DOWN AN OPEN GRID.-5 DAMAGES.—Mrs. Ellen Wainwright, Shaw-street, a small shopkeeper, sued Mr. Thomas D. Livesey, grocer, High-street, for the sum of £5, being damages for injury to her by the alleged negli- gence pf the defendant, or his servants, in leaving the grid to his shop open and unprotected.—Mr. Lake was for the plaintiff, and Mr. H. Linaker for defendant.—Mr. Lake, in opening the case, said there was a grid in front of defend- ant's shop, leading into the cellar. The grid extended a matter of four feet into, and formed part of, the parapet. Next to defendant's was the 'shop of Mrs. James, confec- tioner, whose door was about two yards from the grid. On the 6th May plaintiff bad been to Mrs. James's on business, and on coming outlier attention was drawn to a coal cart standing opposite. The next moment she found herself falling down the grid. She was very much shaken, as she was a stout and elderly woman, and suffered considerable ' pain. She was assisted home, and attended by Dr. McDou- gall. She was obliged to have the assistance of her married daughter, who lives at Frodsham, in order to carry on the business of her shop. She stopped with her three weeks, and the claim was for medical attendant's bill £1 Is., ' daughter for managing the shop £1 Is., and the balance— I 12 18s.—for keeping the daughter and compensation fot pain and suffering attendant upon the accident. At the time when it happened coals were being put down the grid. The place was, in fact, entirely unprotected, and there was nothing whatever to warn passengers coming in that direction, or to call attention to the fact of it being open. After proceedings had been taken the defen- dant called upon the plaintiff and offered to pay the doctor's bill, but nothing more. The claim of £5 was made up asl follows ! medical attendance £1 is, daughter managing the I shop £1 is, and the expense of keeping the daughter and', compensatiqn£2 18s.—The plaintiff was then called, and said that on the 6th May he went to the shopiof Mrs. James, confectioner, High-street, and when coming out turned to her left, for the putpose of going towards home, when she fell down the grid belonging to defendant's place of business, and was very much hurt. She was helped up by a young man named Mr, J. W. Timperley, and went into Mr. Livesey's. Defendant asked her why she had fallen down the grid, and she repliedby enquiring how it was that it was open and unprotected. He did not ask her to sit down; in fact he did not even offer her a drink of water— Dr. McDougall said he was called in by the plaintiff, and found her in a condition perfectly consistent with having met with the accident.—Mr. Timperley then gave evidence, and added that whenever the grid of his father's shop was open it was the custom to protect it.—John Kinsey, a boy, and Ellen Summerfield were hls called.—Mr. Linaker sub- mitted that the plaintiff had not made out a case which ought to entitle her to compensstion.—Her evidence did not show that she had taken ordinary care to see that she was 410 t running into danger. It was the custom in Runcorn and many other towns for the shopkeepers to take goods In- to their cellars by the griels,and defendanthad only followed out the usual pracfice. Coal was being delivered in bags,' and plaintiff admitted that on coming out of Mrs, James's shop she saw the cartagainst the kerbstone, right opposite to where the grid was. In spite of this she did not take the ordinary precaution to see whether the grid was open or not, but deliberately turned round the corner and walked into the opening.—Mr. Lake: There is no corner at the place.— His fienour considered that there ha ;! been negligence clearly proved on the part of the defendant. Whilst Mrs. Livesey was perfectly justified in taking coal into his cellar in the way described, if he did so he WAS bound to put up a rope or some other defence to protect the grid. In this case there was a grid close to another person's shop, and nothing was done to protect customers from going in or out of that esta- blishment. t ven granting that the plaintiff might have been guilty of some negligence, be could not see tkat it was the entire cauSe of the accident. The real question for con- sideration was, what was the immediate cause of the acci- dent? Supposing there had been any protection at all at the place, and the plaintiff had been going out of Mrs. James' shop, taking no care, and had thus tumbled in, that would have made all the difference; but there was no attempt shown on the part of the defendant to put up any protec- tion whatever. It was not a case where the woman had been looking one way and going another at the same time. —Mr. Linaker said that if His Honour held that the plain- tiff had not been guilty of such carelessness as would bar her from claimiag compensation he could not carry the case any further. Upon the auestion of damages he submitted that if plaintiff was paid the money she had te give her daughter, and the medical expenses, it would be quite suffi- cient, under the circumstances.—The Judge remarked that plaintiff was entitled to something beyond this; she ought to receive something as compensation for the injury she had I suffered. There was the keep of the daughler, who was a I married woman, and did not live with her. It was difficult I to reduce the amount of the damages claimed, which were not large, and he should give judgment for plaintiff, £5. payable in a week. He had no doubt that the accident was one which the defendant regretted as much as anybody.— Mr. Linaker : It was simply a question of liability.—The Judge: It is fortunate that it was no worse. ANoTEEE CASE WITITDRAWN.—A case was upon the cause list in which Mr. Denby, clerk to the Widnes School Board, sued Mr. Soulby, master at the Wesleyan Methodist school, for the value of some fixtures.—Mr. Lake and Mr. W H. Linaker were the legal gentlemen concerned ;• and the Judge was informed that the case bad been withdrawn upon terms arranged.

div.head: LORD DERBY ON THE LAND ACT.
div.p: LORD DERBY ON THE LAND ACT.

Lord Derby contribntes to the October number of the Nineteenth Century an article on "Ireland and the Land Act." Speculating on how the Act wilt affect landlords, he maintains that the large absentee owners will suffer very little, if at all, their estates being generally low rented, and they themselves being indifferent to such loss of power as is involved in inability to substitute one tenant for another. The change will be to them nothing. The real sufferer will be the small needy proprietors and landowners, who valued their estates chiefly as a trust put into their hands to im- prove and develope. The former class would be ruined; the latter would find their money wasted and their occupation gone. The Land Commissioners are absolute ss no other set of men in the British isles are. They have no law to guide them, and there is no appeal from their decisions. They are not likely to require the reduction of any rents that have not been raised lately, and this' would be the case over one-half or two-thirds of Ireland. As regards the effect on thejnterests of the tenant, all that is certain is that he will have less done for him, and will be more free to do what he can for himself. The improving landlord will dis- appear, and capital and skill will be scarce. Lord Derby considars that the best prespect for the Irish peasant lies in the direction of emigration. He is not sanguine enough to suppose that the Land Court will satisfy popular expecta- tion. Though he believes the Act will fail as a measure of minciliation, it will probably effectually check the spread of anti-English feeling in Ulster,. and detach many adherents from the National cause. But the principal gain is outside of Ireland, for the Government will have satisfied evvry reasonable man in England and Scotland that the utii limits of just and reasonable concessions to Irish demal have been reached..

BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. pwactea.] No. XVIII. JERICHO. Our second Lord's day in Palestine was spent on the site of ancient Jericho. It was a delightfufday ; the scene from our tents was magnificent ; the once rich and beautiful plain, now lying wild and waste in its tangled luxuriance, was before us, stretching for many miles north and south while, to the east, directly before us, but eight miles away, the Jordan's dark green banks seemed to hang like a fringe at the base of Moab's exquisitely-formed and many-tinted mountains. It was a real enjoyment to watch the ever- changing hues of the hills in the deepening shadows of , eventide and a source of deep interest to recall the eventful scenes which in the long past had transpired within the sweep of mountain and valley spread out before us. In Jericho's palmiest days the view from the city must have been very grand. The plain now a jungle but then in its highest state of cultivation, poured forth' its fruits and various products in the richest abundance. Watered by the swellings of the Jordan, and nurtured by the tropical heat of the sum what a full reward must have crowned the labour of the husbandman, and what a picture of unfailing beauty the landscape must have presented to the eye. But, in the affluence of its fruits, and in the ease with which they were produced, would probably lie the greatest danger to the people. They would IJEI more liaole to sink into luxurious and effeminate habits than in any other part of Palestine. If we are warranted in the conclusion that Rahab was the best specimen of humanity in Jericho, may not the city before its investment by Joshua, have filled up the measure of its iniquity as brimful as Sodom and Gomorrah had done in an age long preceding. This glorious plain was to the Israelites the threshold to the promised land. Over its shining fields and orchards the multitu- dinous seed of Abraham spread their tents after forty years' sojourn in the wilderness, and for centuries made it the gathering place of their tribes. Ruling in the midst of its busy populations, Samuel in his day held assize and judged the people. Ruth, with her widowed mother, travelled on their way to Bethlehem from between the purple mountains yonder, and crossed this plain, then dotted with princely palaces and filled with gardens and orchards, which, according to Josephus, abounded with spices and fruits of the rarest kinds. Ages afterwards the Divine Seed of this lowly Moabitish damsel—He who was at once the Son of David and the Son of God—trod its shining ways, scattering His gifts of healing and blessing as the thousands followed Him along the bank's of the Jordan on His way from Galilee to Jerusalem. Casting back our vision, his- torically, we have over yonder the spot from which the flaming chariot bore the Prophet Elijah into heaven. Then we have, within a few yards of the same spot, the scene of the second Elijah, John the Baptist's labours, whose fervid preaching drew myriads from all parts of Palestine, and among them one whose dignity was so transcendent that the heavens opened to attest His Divinity. Where besides, on this earth's extended surface, is there a plain so rich in sacred associations? A plain over whose bosom has swept such a succession of glorious events? Nor must we lose Bight of the picture which first bursts upon our view as we trace its history on the page of Holy Writ—the raining down of fire and brimstone from the very expanse that opened to receive Elijah, and to proclaim the Divine Majesty of the long expected Messiah! Thus we ponder until our hearts are on fire; and there creeps over them the chilling fact that this same scene, with all its high renown, its magnificent beauty, its astonishing advantages, with a soil rich beyond compare, and with streams of sparkling water rushing down from the mountains across its noble plain, is lying a picture of desolation and unfruitfulness, 'alaich nothing but the lasting curse of heaven—at present embodied in Turkish misrule and oppression—can account • for. At eight o'clock on Monday morning, March 20th, Jericho was left behind, and we passed up through a deep valley into the Quarantania Mountains on our way to Bethel. In a few minutes we began to ascend the steep mountain tracks, and continued W climb from one elevation to another, until in the evening we found ourselves 4.000 feet above the level of the Jordan, and within sight of Jerusalem, at ten or twelve miles distance. The mountains on the way are very beautiful, and command magnificent views. The valleys and table- lands in high altitude seemed capable of fine cultivation, and we could not but think how glorious the country must have looked when these were waving with corn, and the mountains, by which they were sheltered, were covered with the vine, the fig tree, the olive, and the pomegranate. The soil itself appeared to increase in richness as we reached the highest points. Wherever the loose stones which bestrew almost every mountain side had been cleared and formed into thick fences, the rich brown loam contrasted very finely with the white limestone, and gave freshness and variety to the landscape. At noon, we lunched and rested beneath a widely-spreading olive, in view of the ancient mounds of Gibeah, Hai and Mickmash, scenes in which Saul and Jonathan and David played conspicuous parts. As we drew nigh to Bethel, we passed through vineyards en- closed with the thick stone walls I have mentioned, and close to the village we saw finely sculptured stones worked in with clay and rubble that formed the hedges. Grecian capitals, both Corinthian and Doric, thus desecrated, spoke of the alien rule which once devastated the land, but which has so utterly perished that a few stone fragments such as these scattered here and there, are all that remain of the many attempts to stamp a Grceco-Roman character upon its soil.

BETHEL. B:thel is not greatly superior to the other villages in Palestine. It has a few decent houses built with the antiquated bevelled stones whi‘h have been appropriated with vandal-like rude- ness to cover the filth and squalor inseparable from Turkish rule. Hanging about our tents when we arrived were a number of lazy-looking brown fellows of the Arab type. They sat with their feet dangling over the walls of the large old reservoir in the centre of which our tents were spread ; while, in closer proximity we had the usual swarm of beg- ging children following us whenever we left our tents. Near to our encampment was one of those old wells which from time immemorial have been the centres of Eastern life and activity. To this fine spring, whose waters well over its brink as it may have done since the time of of Abraham, a woman came down soon after we arrived, just as women might have done three thousand years ago, dressed in the primitive loose garment of blue serge, and with a pitcher poised on her head. It was a picture so familiar to us through the medium of illustrated Bible history, that we felt as if we had been moving in the midst of these scenes of patriar- chal simplicity all our lives. Before sundown we rambled over the newly ploughed fields, and pitched up bits of tesselated pavement and sundry fossils lying loose on the soil, the one speaking to us of faded and vanished earthly dory, the other of God's wonderful and imperishable work- ing in this physical universe. We were now treading the very ground over which Abraham had reigned in princely affluence and purity of life. Between this place and Hai it was that the flocks of Abraham and Lot pastured until the quarrels of their servants drove those kinsmen asunder, and exposed Lot and his family to the dangers of town life—to the corrupting influences of the "cities of the plain." In the calm of the night as the stars blazed out, we stood outside and pictured to ourselves the lonely stranger from Beersheba lying out, as the Easterns do, with his loose outward garment wrapped entirely over and around him, and with the not essentially oriental stone for his pillow. The seraphic vision that broke upon his slumbers arose vividly before our mind's eye. The celestial ladder, with its angelic throng gliding up and down the shining way, became more of a reality than ever it had done before, and we felt as Jacob did of old, that it was a very Bethel—the House of God and the gate of heaven. Yet we stood on a place which, though had it been exalted to heaven, has been brought down to hell. According to the prediction of Amos, and on account of its idolatries, Bethel "has come to nought." Its ruins cover a space of three or four acres, and are in utter desolation, ploughed over so that scarcely a vestige of its ancient glory is to be seen. My nervous system had got so highly strung that I had no rest until long after daybreak. After getting my pillows finally arranged, I fell into a sound sleep, but soon after awoke to find Abdallah, at once the plague and plaything of our tent life, busily at work rolling up the vacated beds of my companions, who had gone into the fields. I knew it was the signal for pulling dawn the tents, and that in a few minutes I should be left to dress and pack up my things in the open air. Jumping up, I ordered him out as sternly as I could. Looking back over his shoulder to see if I was in earnest, he made his exit. In a very few minutes I had finished dressing. and in five minutes more Abdallah had again entered, given his orders for the tent to be pulled down, whilehe rolled up the bed, and there it lay bundled up on the spot I had so cosily occupied a few moments before. Abdallah was a Turk, and the most audaciously impudent fellow I ever met with. Se.acely had I seated myself on my trunk, when I heard one of the ladies exclaiming, "Go out! I say, go out! I am not ready, go out !" Abdallah had seen, by some means or other, that Miss C.'s toilet was nearly completed, and in spite of all remonstrance had effected an entrance, and was rolling up the beds. Her lady companion and cousin had effected an escape fully equipped, and, with riding-whip in 11:11d, was pacing before the door of the tent, almost dancing n enjoyment, while Miss C. was vainly attempting to oust the intruder.
(To N continued nest week.)

A ROMANTIC Locat WEDDING.—The Leigh Journal says :—A young lady, possessed of considerable wealth in her own right, amounting to about £20,000, and residing for the last few years in a townsUip not a thousand miles from Leigh, recently entered into the marriage state under rather remarkable circumstances. Various rumours have been in the air for months, all tending to show that domestic info- , liCity was in full sway between daughter and stepmother, due apd ,rently to the incompatibility of one or both their temperaments. A horse dealer, hailing from the Warrington district, has recently been paying his addresses to the young lady, and one day laid out a successful scheme for clandestinely marrying her. His lover and her half sister went ' to stay with a relative of his, and whilst there the marriage I took place before the consent of the parents of the bride, who is only 17, had been obtained, and even without I'm k oWledge of the sister staying at the same house. '; o Shock of surprise to the young lady's father place hea shortlyringa nn happily hastenc.,d his death, which took afn.o-wards.

div.p: they could not have any difficulty in answering them. In chemistry also, as well as mathematics, there would be see- siorAl examinations, and questions would be given. The text book would be Kemshead's published by Collins and Sons, at Is., or Roscoe's, which was a more advanced work, issued by Macmillan, at 4s. 6d. If sufficient students joined to make it worth his while to conduct an advanced _ _ _
chemistry class, he would take it separately, at a different hour from the ordinary class. e had now to speak for a moment on the City and Guilds of London Institute. The
council of the guilds were very wishful to advance tech- nical 3ducation in England, feeling no . doubt. that if the
country was to compete with other- nations, the workmen must have technical education; those who laboured in our

... manufactories must know upon what they were working, and thoroughly understand the chemistry of the products they were using, or it was impossible for them to suggest any improvement of the processes in which they were engaged. There were several subjects which he considered might be taken up, including the alkali trade, then brewing, gas and mechanical engineering, iron and steel manufacture, plumbers' work, photographic printing, telegraphy, watch and clock making, tanning leather, and the making of tools. The subject which they intended to teach in connection with the trade guilds, supposing that a class could be formed, was the alkali manufacture. In order that _a candidate might

enter for examination, it was necessary that he should have passed certain examinations In connection with the Science and Art Department, or the authorities would not grant him a full technological certificate, but only a preliminary one, which would be extended to a full one upon the examina- tions being passed. The examinations necessary for the alkali manufacture were the last two of the follawing sub-

jects in the elementary stage :—Building construction, and drawing, theoretical, chemistry, acoustics, light and heat. The examinations were held in exactly the same manner as those by the Science and Art Department, but instead of there being three grades there were only two,—the honours and the passed. Any candidate who satisfied the examiners would either get a first or a second class, according to the merit of his paper. In addition to these classes there were in the honours' stages two prizes offered. The first was the silver medal and £5; and the second a bronze medal and .£5. In the passed grade there were five prizes, the first being a silver medal and £3; the second a bronze medal and £3; the third a bronze medal and £2; the fourth a bronze medal and £1; and the fifth a bronze medal. The subjects in- cluded a knowledge of some raw material, such as lime, sulphuric acid, salt cake, hydrochloric acid, black ash, caustic soda, bicarbonate, bleaching powder, and silver re- covery. He would have to describe the plant and operations as minutely as possible. The teaching would be carried on Iby some chemical experiments; and by visits to works, if they could arrange with some gentleman to give them the opportunities. No one was allowed to enter unless they were employed in alkali works, or some manufactory closely con- nected witli them, but it did not matter how they were en- gaged, whether in the office, the laboratory, or the yard. There were no very cheap text books for this subject. Those which might be used at the commencement of the session were Roscoe's Technical Chemistry, Kemshead's work on the alkali trade, published at 12s. 6d., and some dearer pub- lications. He hoped this session would be very successful, and put all the science classes of Runcorn on a far better footing than they ever were before. Before sitting down he wished to thank those students who were connected with the classes last session for their attendance, and their behaviour. During the course they gave him their attention, and the majority of them worked very well. They ought all to feel very much obliged to the committee for their labours, and also to Mr. Lyon for the part he had taken. That gentle- man had bad considerable work to do in connection with the classes, and The had never hesitated at putting himself to any inconvenience so that they might go on successfully. If nothing more resulted from the present session than from the last, he (Mr. Tate) should be perfectly content, for he should feel convinced that the knowledge gained would be found quite equal to the work done, and that at least he should not have laboured in vain. (Applause.) Mr. T. Simmer was next called upon' and remarked that it appeared to him that there was a lack of knowledge of building construction amongst workmen generally, and one of the objects for which the classes were established was to give this instruction. He found that too frequently a man did a certain job after a certain fashion because he saw others do it in the same way, and not because he knew anything of the principles connected with it. If a workman had a know- ledge of the principles of construction, he was sure to work much more intelligently, because he then knew why a poet was put in a certain position or a stone cut in a certain form. Having given one or two instances of this lack of technical information on the part of workmen, the speaker went on to say that the possession of it would un- doubtedly enable a man to do his work with more satisfac- tion to himself and to his employer. He was very pleased to see so large an attendance' and he hoped the session would provd a highly successful one. Mr. Tate had every reason to congratelate himself upon the success of his last class, and he hoped that he would have a like success in the future. ( Applause.) The CHAIRMAN complimented the gentlemen on ,the admirable and perspicuous manner in which they had ex- plained the nature of the classes to the meeting. He then proceeded to say that for some years past there had been a good deal of talk about the supremacy of Britain as a manufacturing nation being on the wane • that the conti- nental nations were outrunning us, and taking the markets of the world from us by the superiority of their manufac- tures, and through being able to do things better than we did them. It would, however, seem from the Board of Trade returns that there was not very much ground for the asser- tion. There was no doubt that in certain things continen- tal nations did excel us, but in most matters Great Britain was holding her own ; and he felt sure that when the science and art classes which had been and were being established throughout the country, brought to maturity the good seed which had been sown, there was not the slightest doubt that England would not only be able to hold her present proud position but even go beyond it. (Applause.) It was quite • true that in the past technological knowledge in France and Germany had been in advance, of that possessed by the ; workpeople of our own land, but this state of things was being rapidly altered by the work which was being carried on all through the kingdom under the auspices of the Science and Art Department at South Kensington and the City of London Guilds and Institute. On the motion of Mr. Jontescier (organist), a hearty vote of thanks was given to Mr. Lyon for his services in the past ; and the public proceedings terminated.

Samuel Whitley, a young man, was brought up in custody charged with being found in an outhouse in Heath-road, belonging to John Bradburn.—The complainant said about six o'clock on Sunday morning he found that the lock of the stable door had been forced off. He opened the door and shouted out "Who's there ?" The prisoner ran out and tried to push him down. He reasoned with him, saying that he ought to be glad to be allowed to stay there. He then jumped over the wall into the road, and began to swear and say that if he would come into the road he would kick his I head off. He went on in that way for about five minutes, when he awoke his nephew named Sweeney, who was in the I house, and they followed the prisoner down the road. They had a struggle together, and after a short time the prisoner pulled out a knife, and said he would give it to them if he I would let him go. His nephew knocked it out of his hand, ifearing he might injure one of them with it, and the priso- ner again began to struggle. He then said that if they I would let him go he would give them his belt. He pulled off a heavy volunteer's belt, but instead of giving it to them be began to strike them furiously. While this was going on he fell on his back, and Sweeney and he then took hold of him. The struggle continued, and besides hurting his , nephew with his efforts to get away, he also bit him ' (witness) slightly on the thumb. He gave him in charge.— The Chairman said the case was a bad one, and there being la black list against the prisoner, he would have to go to i prison for two months with hard labour. THE SALVATION ARMY.'

On Tuesday, a preliminary meeting was held in the Lecture Room of the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association to consider the formation of classes in mathe- matics, building construction, inorganic chemistry, and technology of the alkali trade, in connection with the Science and Art Department and the City and Guilds of London Institute. Mr. Wm. Lyon presided, and there was a large attendance. The CRAIR3IAN briefly introduced the subject to the meeting, which, he said, was a preliminary one, called for the purpose of getting up classes in science. During the last session Mr. Tate had passed a very fair proportion of his students, and had himself been successful in winning the highest prize open, viz., the silver medal and £5. (Ap- plause.) Without any further remarks he would call upon that gentleman to give them some details in reference to the work proposed to be carried out. • Mr. F. H. TOTE (chemist at Messrs. Hazlehurst and Sons) said that in the autumn of 1879 a committee was formed in Runcorn for the purpose of conducting classes in connection with the Science and Art Department. The idea originated with some members of the club which had been formed by gentlemen connected with the Literary and Mechanics' Institute, for the purpose of studying botany, which Mr. Robinson, of Frodsham, undertook to teach. In the same year the committee of Holy Trinity Church formed classes under the superintendence of Mr. Annett, and those present would see, from bills in the windows, that he was continuing them. The botany and chemistry classes met at the rooms of the institute, and had a fair amount of success. Last year, Mr. Drummond having left the town, and Mr. Robin- son not being disposed to continue his work of teaching, a class in chemistry was started under himself (the speaker). Twenty-four members were enrolled, which was a consider- able increase. For some time the attendance was excellent,l and during the session averaged about 16. In May, how- ever, only nine sat for examination, of which three obtained Queen's prizes, three first-class certificates, and two second- I class certificates. .Under the same committee, an examina- tion was held in connection with the City and Guilds of , London Institute. Four candidates sat, and two passed.' This session, owing to being unable to rent the rooms in con- nection with the institute, the gentlemen interested in the classes had made application for the lecture room at the Young Men's Christian Association. They had not received permission from the committee to hold the meetings there, but they would assemble next week, and there was not much doubt that the application would be , granted. It was intended to have classes for teaching build- I ing construction, mathametics, chemistry and alkali manufacture. The classes would be in association with the Science and Art Department, South Kensington, acting under the Committee of Council on Education, the president being Earl Spencer. This department was formerly under the Board of Trade, but some years since if passed into the hands of the Committee of Council on Education. Money was voted annually to the council by Parliament, and a cer- tain sum which they had to distribute for the purposes of furthering education in the country. A portion of this was voted to the Science and Art department, South Kensington, who did all they could to establish classes throughout the THE a SERAPHIC DOCTOR OF country for the teaching of art, such as freehand drawing, perspective, and geometry; and, in addition to these, there WARRING-TON. were some 23 or 24 art subjects, in which instruction was given. GOLBORNE.

THE Macs Lurr.—At the Newton petty sessions. on Satur- day, before Colonel McCorquodale, Messrs. J. Pearson, R. Houghton, and T. Comber, James Sharratt, collier, Bamfur- long, was summoned for obstructing Police-constable Beards- worth whilst in the execution of his duty.—.-The °Nicer stated that about two o'clock on Sunday, the 11th ultimo, be went to execute a warrant upon a man named Clubb, when defendant interfered and incited Clubb to kick the constable.—Defendant pleaded not guilty, and said be be- lieved Clubb was being punished by the handcuffs, and he only wanted the officer to "slacken" them.—Fined 10s. and costs.—William Shaughnessy and Patrick Flinn, colliers, Golborne, were charged with being drunk and causing a dis- turbance in the Prince of 11 ales public-honse.— P.C. Beardsworth stated that on Sunday evening the 14th ultimo, he was passing the house about 8-20, when be saw defendants drunk and fighting.—Shaughnessy, who admitted the charge, was mulcted in the sum of 55. and costs. Flinn did not appear, and a warrant was granted for his ap- prension.—Jane Howard and Ellen Howard, factory opera- tives, Golborne, were smmmoned for committing a breach. of the peace.—Police-constable Beardsworth said he was passing Messrs. Brewis' mill about a quarter to nine on the 16th ult., when he saw a large crowd assembled and the two defendants quarrelling. They were making use of foul language. .He had to remove them from the street as they refused to desist. Defendants caused considerable amusement in court by the determined attempt of one to throw the blame upon ithe other.—Ordered to pay the costs, and bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months.

SPECIAL ANNOUNCEMENT. 5.000 MAGNIFICENT PRESENTS TO BE GIVEN AWAY. THE ANGLO-FRENCH JEWELLERY COMPANY, in order to introduce their business before the public, have, at enormous expetise, resolved to present to every person applying for the same, a FRENCIi POCKET TIME INDICATOR (Patented). This admirable little article 15 the size and shape of an ordi- nary watch, has strong metal cases, steel works, balanced action, enamelled dial, crystal glass dome, patent adjusting swivel ring for attaching to watch guard, each denotes correct solar time, and in fact no one, either male or female, should want for a watch, when such an opportunity as this offers; a chance will never occur again. The time Indicator is warranted for five years. To secure one of i,hese little articles the sum of Is 4d must be forwarded either in P 0.0. or stamps. or two will be sent tor 2s sd, with the full name and address filled in the form below, and enclosed to the Anglo-French Jewellery Co., Matlock House, Sparkhill, Birmingham. A handsome gilt to every purchaser. We have resolved to give away, with every Pocket, Timepiece, a neat and useful companion, in Aluminium Gold case, suitable for lady or gentleman. None sold without this coupon.

Address.—The MANAGER, Anglo-French Jewellery Company, Matlock House, Sparkhill, Birmingham. LAPORTANT.—As the quantity is limited, intending pur- chasers are requested to send at once. Orders received after these are sold will be returned.

ADVERTISEMENT OF SUSPENSION. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Chief Registrar of Friendly Societies has, pursuant to 38 and 39 Vic., c. 60, s. 12, by writing under his hand, dated the 23rd tay of September, 1881, SUSPENDED for three months the REGISTRY of the POOR MAN'S FRIENDLY BURIAL SOCIETY (Register No. 1,800) held at the White Horse Inn, 41, Naylor-street, St. Helens, in the county of Lancaster, on the ground that the Society has wilfully, and after notice from a Registrar, violated the provisions of the above-mentioned Act in respect of the valuation of its assets and liabilities. The Society ceases to enjoy (during such suspension) the privileges of a registered society, but without prejudice to any liability incurred by the Society, which may be enforced against it as if such suspension had not taken place. E. W. BRABROOK, Acting as Chief Registrar. - -- ST. HELENS PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY. SESION 1881-2.
